story.title: Max, Sami, and the Click Heard Round the World
story.subtitle: A LEGO history adventure, one brick at a time

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Workshop in Billund (1932)
chapters.text:
Saturday night, long after lights-out, Max lay on the carpet with a half-built LEGO Technic robot arm, a red motor humming between his fingers.

Sami sat cross-legged nearby, sketching the robot arm in her notebook, adding gears that did not exist yet.

"Bet I finish the gear train before you finish drawing it," Max said.

"Bet you don't," Sami said, not looking up.

The little motor buzzed, and a stray brick on the carpet buzzed back. It glowed soft green, like a firefly caught under plastic.

Max froze. Sami's pencil stopped mid-line.

The brick rolled over, clicked onto itself twice — **CLICK. CLICK.** — and stood up on four stubby legs. Two eyes made of light blinked open.

"Evening," said the brick-robot, in a voice like two pieces snapping together. "Name's Brik. Built from spare Technic parts and about ninety years of plastic history. Want to see where you came from?"

Max looked at Sami. Sami looked at Max.

"Define 'where,'" Max said.

Brik's eye-lights flickered like he was smiling. He clicked his four legs together, and the floor between them opened into a tunnel lined with studs, like the world's longest brick road.

"Billund, Denmark," Brik said. "1932. Pack a jacket. It's cold where carpenters work."

They landed in a small wooden workshop that smelled like sawdust and fresh paint. A man with sleeves rolled to his elbows was sanding the leg of a stepladder.

"That's **Ole Kirk Christiansen**," Brik said. "He started this whole company **in Billund, Denmark, in 1932** — making wooden toys and stepladders, because times were hard and people needed both."

Sami picked up a little wooden duck from the workbench, its wheels painted bright red. "He made toys AND ladders? Same guy?"

"Same guy," Brik said. "A carpenter needed money however he could get it."

Max turned the duck over, checking the axle. "The wheels actually roll. He cared about it working, not just looking nice."

Ole Kirk looked up, surprised to see two kids and a glowing robot in his workshop, then laughed and handed Sami a scrap of wood to sand herself.

"Every toy I make," he said, "has to work and has to be loved. If it only does one, I throw it out and start again."

Sami grinned and kept sanding. The duck's wheel spun true.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well (1934)
chapters.text:
Two years later, by Brik's clock, the workshop had a brand-new sign going up over the door.

A painter balanced on a short ladder, lettering slow gold letters: L-E-G-O.

"LEGO?" Sami read aloud. "What's that even mean?"

"**'Leg godt,'**" Brik said. "Danish for **'play well.'** Ole Kirk shortened it **in 1934** and it stuck."

Max tapped his chin, the way he did before a trick question. "Didn't I read somewhere it also means something in Latin?"

Brik's eye-lights dimmed, like he was choosing his words carefully. "Good catch. Some people say **'lego' means 'I put together' in Latin**, too. Kind of perfect for a toy that snaps together, right?"

"So that's why he picked it," Max said, already pleased with himself.

"Actually — probably not," Brik said. "It's a fun coincidence people like to repeat. Nobody's found proof Ole Kirk even knew that Latin word. Good story. Shaky history."

Max's face fell for half a second, then he shrugged. "Still cool."

The painter climbed down and stepped back to admire his work. Sami copied the gold letters into her sketchbook, looping the O's extra round.

"Write it bigger," Brik said. "This name's going to end up on every continent."

Sami grinned and did exactly that, her pencil pressing so hard it nearly tore the page.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Machine That Changed Everything (1947)
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled nothing like sawdust. It smelled like hot metal, sharp and strange, almost like melted crayons.

A huge black machine sat in the middle of the workshop, taller than Ole Kirk himself, with a funnel on top and a mold clamped at the front.

Max's hands actually shook a little. "Is that an **injection molding machine**? That pushes melted plastic into a mold, and it comes out solid, right?"

"Exactly," Brik said. "**In 1947**, Ole Kirk's company became one of the very first in Denmark to own one. Everybody thought plastic was a fad. He bet the whole workshop on it instead."

The machine hissed, and a tray slid out holding small studded rectangles, still warm.

Sami picked one up carefully and turned it over in her fingers. "They're hollow underneath. Like little houses with no floor."

"Good eye," Brik said. "**In 1949** they're called **Automatic Binding Bricks** — the very first ancestor of the brick in your pocket right now, Max."

Max checked his pocket. Sure enough, a stray brick from his Technic set sat there, dusty from the carpet.

He held the old brick and the new brick side by side. They were almost the same, except the old one's studs looked a little looser, a little less sure of themselves.

"They don't click, though," Max said, pressing two together. They wobbled apart. "Something's missing."

Brik's eyes flickered, impressed. "Hang onto that thought. Someone's about to fix exactly that problem."

Sami was already sketching the hollow brick in her notebook, a question mark scribbled where the studs met underneath.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tubes That Changed Everything Twice (1958)
chapters.text:
Nine years later, by Brik's reckoning, they stood in a brighter, busier factory room. A young man with the same sharp eyes as Ole Kirk hunched over a worktable, muttering while two bricks wobbled apart in his hands.

"That's **Godtfred Kirk Christiansen**," Brik said. "Ole Kirk's son. He's got the same problem you had, Max. The bricks hold shape. They don't hold together."

Godtfred groaned and tried again. Wobble. Apart.

Sami leaned over his shoulder and peered underneath an empty brick. "What if there was something under here," she said, "little tubes, to grab the bumps on the brick below?"

Godtfred's head snapped up. "Say that again."

Sami said it again, slower, and sketched it right there on his notepad: a ring of little tubes hanging inside the brick's empty belly.

Max grabbed two of the prototype bricks and pressed one onto the other, hard. **CLICK.** He pulled. It held.

"IT HOLDS!" Max shouted, forgetting entirely that he was supposed to be the calm one.

Godtfred laughed and shook both their hands like they'd just saved his whole company, which, in a way, they had.

"The official paperwork goes in **on January 28th, 1958**," Brik said. "That's called a **patent** — it's a certificate that says 'this invention belongs to us, officially.' And here's the wild part: a brick made that day still clicks perfectly onto a brick made today. The design barely changed in almost seventy years."

Max turned the old brick and his own Technic brick over, side by side. They fit like they'd always known each other.

"No wonder you never throw bricks away," Sami said.

"Never," Max agreed, already plotting what to build when they got home.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Starting Fresh (1960)
chapters.text:
Two years on, the factory yard looked different: a warehouse standing empty, its wooden shelves gone, the smell of smoke still faint in the air.

"What happened here?" Sami asked quietly.

"**In 1960**, a fire burned through the warehouse where they kept the wooden toys," Brik said. "Nobody was hurt. But years of wooden ducks and stepladders were gone."

Max looked at the empty space where shelves used to stand. "That's rough."

"It was," Brik said. "But the family looked at what was still standing — the plastic brick machines — and made a choice. No more wood. Plastic, all the way."

Sami tilted her head. "So the fire kind of... decided for them?"

"Sort of," Brik said. "Sometimes a hard thing clears room for the right thing."

Three years later, by Brik's count, they stood in a lab room full of brick samples in a rainbow of colors, laid out on a long table.

A scientist in a white coat held up two bricks, one old and a little yellowed, one newer and brilliantly red.

"**In 1963**," Brik said, "they switched to a tougher plastic called **ABS** — it doesn't crack as easily, and it keeps its color instead of going dull and yellow."

Max picked up the old yellowed brick and held it next to the bright red one. "So this old one's basically sunburned."

"Basically," Brik said.

Sami sketched both bricks side by side in her notebook, labeling the new one TOUGH in blocky letters.

"Good instinct," said the scientist, who hadn't spoken until now, and smiled at the two of them before going back to her samples.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Park Next Door (1968)
chapters.text:
The next stop had rides.

Real ones — a miniature train chugging past brick castles built taller than Max, crowds of families wandering between them.

"Welcome to **LEGOLAND**," Brik said. "**Opened in Billund in 1968**, right next to the original factory. Built entirely out of —"

"Bricks," Max finished, grinning up at a tiny brick-built mountain carving. "Obviously."

Sami wandered toward a play table where bricks sat fatter and rounder than usual, easy enough for even a toddler to grab.

"These are huge," she said, picking one up. "A baby could hold these without even chewing on them weird."

"That's the idea," Brik said. "**DUPLO**, **introduced in 1969**, built bigger so little hands can manage them — and they still click onto regular bricks, so nobody outgrows the box."

Max tried fitting a DUPLO stud into a regular brick. It slid on, snug as anything. "No way. Same family, different size."

"Same family," Brik agreed. "LEGO never likes leaving anyone out of the click."

A small kid nearby stacked three DUPLO blocks into a wobbly tower and beamed like he'd built a skyscraper. Sami gave him a thumbs up, and he gave one right back, nearly toppling his tower doing it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Gears, Faces, and a New Boss (1977)
chapters.text:
Max practically sprinted into the next room, because it was full of gears.

Real moving gears, axles, beams — a brick skeleton of a crane lifting a block off the floor.

"**LEGO Technic**," Brik said, "**launched in 1977**. Gears and axles instead of just studs. Stuff that actually moves."

Max grabbed a beam and clicked an axle through it, and the little crane's arm swung, slow and smooth. "This is basically robotics. This is where robotics started for me."

"Pretty much," Brik said. "You've got good company."

Sami, meanwhile, had found a tiny yellow figure standing on the table, barely as tall as her thumb. It had a round head, a smiling painted face, and arms that actually bent at the elbow.

"Whoa. Its face comes off?" She lifted the hat and swapped it for a tiny brick helmet from a nearby bin.

"**The first minifigures showed up in 1978**," Brik said. "Movable arms, swappable heads and hats. Before that, LEGO people were just stiff little blobs."

Sami lined up five minifigures in different hats and gave each one a different pretend job: astronaut, chef, brick mason who builds bricks inside a world made of bricks.

A man walked past them with a boy about Max's age trailing behind, both carrying brick boxes stacked past their chins.

"That's **Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen**," Brik said. "Ole Kirk's grandson. **He took charge of the whole company in 1979** — grew up playing with these very bricks, and never really stopped."

Max watched the boy trip slightly over a loose brick and laugh it off. "Guess it runs in the family. Falling over your own toys."

"Occupational hazard," Brik said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Tiny Tires and Big Screens (1999)
chapters.text:
The next room was stacked floor to ceiling with small black rubber tires, more than either kid could count.

Sami grabbed a double handful and let them fall through her fingers like confetti. "Why does one toy company need THIS many tires?"

"Funny thing," Brik said. "LEGO makes so many tiny rubber tires that some people joke it's one of the biggest tire makers in the world, by count — not by actual size. Nobody's driving a car on LEGO tires."

"That's a cheat," Max said, laughing anyway. "But I respect the hustle."

They turned a corner into a room glowing with movie posters: spaceships, laser swords, brick starfighters frozen mid-flight.

"**In 1999**, LEGO put out its **first Star Wars sets**," Brik said. "First time they built sets based on somebody else's movie instead of just their own ideas."

Sami stood on tiptoe to study a brick-built starfighter. "They're really good at turning other people's cool stuff into bricks."

"They're good at turning anything into bricks," Brik corrected. "Around the year 2000, big magazines even named the brick itself a **Toy of the Century** — best toy of the whole hundred years."

Max crossed his arms, pretending to be unimpressed, and completely failing. "Okay. That's deserved."

Sami was already sketching a brick lightsaber, shading the blade in careful pencil strokes, tongue poking out the side of her mouth the way it did when she really meant it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Hard Years (2004)
chapters.text:
The next room was quieter. Shelves half-empty, boxes stacked in uneven piles, nobody rushing around.

"**In the early 2000s**, the company hit a hard patch," Brik said. "They'd spent money on too many different ideas at once, and almost ran out before any of it paid off."

Sami frowned at the empty shelves. "Did they... stop?"

"Close," Brik said. "But not quite. **In 2004**, a new leader named **Jorgen Vig Knudstorp** took over, and he did something simple: he got everybody to focus back on the thing that actually worked."

"The brick," Max said.

"The brick," Brik agreed. "Fewer wild ideas, more good bricks. It worked."

The shelves around them seemed to fill back in as they spoke, boxes stacking themselves higher, color returning to the walls like someone had flipped the lights back on.

Then the whole room went dark, and a giant screen flickered on overhead, bright with brick-built heroes mid-adventure.

"**2014**," Brik said. "**The LEGO Movie** hit theaters. Made entirely out of bricks, about bricks, for people who love bricks. Did way better than anybody expected."

Max watched a brick spaceship burst apart into a thousand satisfying pieces on screen. "That was awesome," he muttered, half to himself.

"Don't get a tune stuck in your head," Brik warned. Too late. Sami was already humming something, grinning the whole time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Back Home
chapters.text:
The tunnel of studs spun them back the way they'd come, past wooden ducks and plastic molds and brick castles, until the carpet reappeared under their knees.

They were home. Same bedroom, same half-built Technic robot arm, same sketchbook open to a half-finished page.

"One more thing," Brik said, his eye-lights steady now. "**The company's still in Billund, Denmark**, right where Ole Kirk's workshop used to stand. And the family that started it all, the **Kirkbi family**, still owns most of it today."

"Same spot," Sami said. "The whole time."

"Same spot," Brik agreed. "Some things are worth keeping."

Max looked down at his robot arm, then at the ancient little brick still sitting in his palm, the one from 1949, loose studs and all. He pressed it onto his newest Technic beam. It clicked, snug and sure, like it had been waiting ninety years for exactly this.

"Still fits," he said.

Sami added one last line to her sketch: two kids, a small glowing robot, and a brick road curling off the edge of the page into the dark.

Brik's legs folded, and he clicked himself back into one ordinary-looking brick on the carpet, green light fading to nothing.

Max picked it up and set it carefully on his shelf, right next to the robot arm.

"Think he'll come back?" Sami asked, already yawning.

"Bricks always come back," Max said. "That's kind of the whole point."

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a whole robot arm left to finish.

story.title: Ada and the Magnet That Wouldn't Let Go
story.subtitle: A fridge-magnet adventure with Bolt the robot

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Wiggling Letters
chapters.text:
Ada lay on her bedroom floor, lining up fridge magnet letters to spell her name. A. D. A.

Her toy robot, Bolt, sat nearby, his round glass eyes dark and quiet.

She reached for the letter B, to spell BOLT next. But it jumped out of her hand. **SNAP!** It stuck straight onto the A.

"Whoa!" said Ada. "Why do some letters jump together, and some just sit there?"

Bolt's eyes blinked blue, waking up. "Every magnet has two ends," he said. "We call them **poles** — a north pole and a south pole. That's where the pull is strongest."

Ada flipped the B around. This time it pushed away instead of snapping.

"Matching poles push apart," said Bolt. "North pushes north. South pushes south. But north and south? They stick like best friends."

Ada tested every letter on the carpet, flipping and flipping. "Stick and flip!" she giggled, finding the pattern all by herself.

Bolt's chest popped open like a tiny door. "Climb in," he said. "I know somewhere tiny you need to see."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside the Invisible Push
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH.** Ada shrank down, smaller than a crumb, standing beside a giant fridge magnet.

She couldn't see anything around it. But her hair stood up and tingled.

"That's the **magnetic field**," said Bolt. "An invisible space around a magnet, where its pulling and pushing happens."

"Invisible? Then how do we know it's really there?" asked Ada.

Bolt sprinkled tiny metal specks, called iron filings, onto the magnet. They lined up in curvy paths, looping from one end to the other.

Ada gasped. "It's like the magnet is drawing with its own push!"

"You found it," said Bolt. "Those curvy lines show exactly where the field goes."

Ada traced one curvy line with her finger, all the way around, grinning the whole time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Tiny Spinning Team
chapters.text:
Deep inside the magnet, Ada heard a hum, like a thousand tiny tops spinning.

"What's making that noise?" she asked.

"Tiny bits inside atoms, called electrons," said Bolt. "Atoms are what everything is made of, even you. Each electron spins around like its own itty-bitty magnet."

Ada peeked closer. Clumps of these tiny magnets pointed the same way, like a crowd doing one dance move.

"Those clumps are called **domains**," said Bolt. "When enough domains point the same way, the whole thing becomes one strong magnet."

"Then why doesn't my wooden block stick?" Ada asked.

"In wood, the tiny magnets point every which way," said Bolt. "All mixed up. No team, no magnet."

Ada nodded slowly. "They need to work together. Like tug-of-war, but everyone pulling the same side."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Rock That Grabbed a Sandal
chapters.text:
**CLICK.** The scene changed. Ada stood on a rocky hillside, long, long ago, near a place called Magnesia.

A shepherd stared down at his sandal, stuck fast to a rock.

"That rock is a **lodestone**," said Bolt. "A magnet that just forms in the ground. People found it right here, ages ago."

"Is that where the word *magnet* comes from?" guessed Ada.

"Good guess," said Bolt. "Lots of people think the name magnet came from this very spot."

Ada picked up a tiny lodestone pebble and held it near her letter B. It wiggled toward it, just a little.

"It really works!" she laughed, tucking it into her pocket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Stubborn Sliver
chapters.text:
The hillside spun into mist. Ada found herself on a wooden ship, long ago, near China.

A sailor held a floating sliver of lodestone in a bowl of water. It slowly turned, pointing the same way every time.

"What's he doing?" whispered Ada.

"Finding his way," said Bolt. "More than two thousand years ago, people floated lodestones to make the very first compasses. It always points the same way, so sailors never got lost."

Ada spun the little sliver herself. It turned right back to the same spot, every single time.

"It's stubborn!" Ada said. "In a good way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Whole Planet is a Magnet
chapters.text:
"Want to know why that sliver always points the same way?" asked Bolt.

"Yes!" said Ada.

**WHOOOOSH** — they zoomed up high, until the whole Earth hung below them like a blue marble.

"Deep down in the middle of Earth," said Bolt, "swirling melted iron makes the whole planet act like one giant magnet."

Ada's mouth dropped open. "The whole Earth is a magnet?"

"Every compass needle lines up with it," said Bolt. "That's why it always points toward Earth's north."

Ada held up her little lodestone pebble. It pointed the same way as before.

"It's listening to the whole planet," she whispered.
chapters.shout_line: THE WHOLE EARTH IS A MAGNET!

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Magnet You Can Switch Off
chapters.text:
They landed in a buzzing workshop, full of wires and bells.

"Watch this," said Bolt. He wrapped a wire into loops, called a **coil**, around a nail. Then he touched both ends to a battery.

**CLICK.** The nail snapped up a handful of paper clips.

"Whoa, the nail wasn't even a magnet before!" said Ada.

"It's called an **electromagnet**," said Bolt. "Wire coiled up, with electricity running through. Turn off the power..." He pulled the wire away. The paper clips dropped. "...and the magnet turns off too."

"Where do people use those?" asked Ada.

"Doorbells, loudspeakers, even giant cranes that lift old cars at the junkyard," said Bolt.

Ada grinned. "Bolt, are you an electromagnet too?"

"Nope," he beeped. "I'm just charming."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH.** Ada landed back on her bedroom carpet, letters scattered around her.

"One more trick," said Bolt. He took her bar-shaped magnet and snapped it in half.

Ada flinched, waiting for one half to lose its pull.

But both pieces still stuck to the fridge. "They both still have a north and a south!" she cheered.

"Every piece becomes its own full magnet," said Bolt. "Snap it a hundred times, still works."

Ada picked up her bendy fridge magnets, the rubbery kind that spelled her name. "Is this why these bend without falling apart?"

"Yup," said Bolt. "Rubber mixed with magnet powder. Bendy and sticky, both at once."

Ada yawned and pressed her A-D-A letters back onto the fridge door, where they held tight. Bolt's eyes dimmed to a sleepy glow beside her.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Stick and flip, and sleep tight.

fact_pack.summary: Magnets are objects that pull on iron and a few other metals using an invisible force called magnetism. This pack explains why magnets attract and repel, how Earth itself is a giant magnet, and the people and discoveries behind our understanding of magnetism.

facts.text: A magnet has two ends called poles, a north pole and a south pole, where the magnetic force is strongest.
Opposite poles attract each other (north pulls south), while like poles repel each other (north pushes north away).
Magnetism comes from the movement of tiny particles called electrons inside atoms, which act like tiny spinning magnets themselves.
In magnetic materials like iron, nickel, and cobalt, groups of atoms called magnetic domains can line up in the same direction to create a strong overall magnetic field.
In most materials the atoms' tiny magnetic fields point in random directions, which is why most objects, like wood or plastic, are not magnetic.
A magnetic field is the invisible area around a magnet where its force can push or pull on other magnetic objects.
You can see the shape of a magnetic field by sprinkling iron filings near a magnet; they line up in curved lines from pole to pole.
The ancient Greeks discovered a naturally magnetic rock called lodestone near a region called Magnesia, which is likely where the word 'magnet' comes from.
The Chinese used lodestones to make the first compasses more than 2,000 years ago, helping travelers find direction.
Earth itself acts like a giant bar magnet because of swirling liquid iron deep in its core, and this is called Earth's magnetic field.
A compass needle points north because it lines up with Earth's magnetic field, with its north pole attracted toward the planet's magnetic north.
Confusingly, Earth's magnetic north pole actually behaves like a magnetic south pole, which is why opposite-pole attraction pulls compass needles there.
In 1820, Danish scientist Hans Christian Oersted discovered that electricity flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field, linking electricity and magnetism for the first time.
English scientist Michael Faraday showed in 1831 that moving a magnet near a wire could create electric current, an idea now used in generators that make our electricity.
An electromagnet is a magnet made by wrapping wire into a coil and running electric current through it, and it can be switched on and off.
Electromagnets are used in everyday things like doorbells, loudspeakers, electric motors, and giant cranes that lift old cars in junkyards.
If you cut a bar magnet in half, you do not get a separate north piece and south piece; each new piece becomes its own smaller magnet with both a north and south pole.
Heating a magnet to a very high temperature, called its Curie point, can make it lose its magnetism because the heat jumbles up its lined-up atoms.
Not all metals are magnetic: for example, aluminum, gold, copper, and silver are not attracted to ordinary magnets.
Some of the strongest magnets made today are called neodymium magnets, made from a mix of iron, boron, and the rare-earth metal neodymium.
Maglev trains use powerful magnets to float above their tracks and glide forward without touching the rails, reducing friction and allowing very high speeds.
Hospitals use giant, extremely strong magnets inside MRI machines to take detailed pictures inside the human body without any cutting.
Some animals, like birds, sea turtles, and some fish, are believed to sense Earth's magnetic field to help them navigate during long migrations.
Refrigerator magnets are usually made from flexible rubber mixed with magnetic powder, which is why they can bend without losing their stick.

story.title: Nora and the Tile That Remembered Pompeii
story.subtitle: A quiet journey to a buried Roman town, one tiny tile at a time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tile That Woke Up
chapters.text:
Nora was lying on her bedroom floor, way past bedtime, pressing the last glass tile into her mosaic. Each tiny square was called a **tessera** — just a fancy word for one little mosaic tile.

She pressed the last red tessera into place. It didn't just sit there. It glowed, warm as a nightlight, and hummed a tiny hum.

"Finally," said a small voice. "I thought you'd never finish the pattern."

Nora sat up fast. The voice was coming from the tile.

"I'm Tessera," it said. "Want to see where mosaics like me come from? Hold on tight."

The floor rippled like water. Nora's bedroom melted into sunlight, dust, and a street made of huge stone blocks.

She looked down and nearly tripped. Raised stones, big as footstools, crossed the road in a row, leaving gaps between them.

"Why put rocks in the middle of a street?" Nora asked.

"Guess," said Tessera.

Nora crouched by a gap. "So people could step across without getting their sandals wet," she said. "And carts could still roll through — the wheels just fit between the stones."

"Exactly right," said Tessera. "Pompeii's streets really did have **stepping stones** like that, so people could cross without stepping in mud, while cart wheels passed through the gaps."

Nora hopped from stone to stone like hopscotch, all the way across. "This town already feels like it was built by someone clever," she said.

"You have no idea," said Tessera. "Come on. Let's go meet it properly."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Five Villages, One Town
chapters.text:
The street opened into a square full of noise. People haggled over fish. A baker balanced bread on a board. A fountain spouted water nearby.

"This town is packed," Nora said, looking around at the crowd.

"About **eleven to fifteen thousand people** lived here," said Tessera, "with shops and bathhouses and theaters and temples, all squeezed into one busy town."

Nora tried to picture that many people. "That's like a hundred classrooms," she said. "Maybe more."

She noticed painted words on a wall, bright red letters. "Is that... an advertisement?" she asked.

"People painted messages right on their walls," said Tessera, "ads for shops, even names of people they wanted to win elections."

Nora laughed. "Walls were like phones."

"Pretty much," said Tessera. "Now — do you know where the name Pompeii comes from?"

Nora thought about her mosaic, how lots of separate tiles joined to make one picture. "Did a few little villages join together to make one big town?" she guessed.

"Close," said Tessera. "People think the name may come from a very old word meaning **five** — maybe because five small villages joined to build Pompeii."

"Five pieces, one town," Nora said. "Just like my mosaic. Five tiles, one sun."

Tessera's glow brightened, pleased. "You really do think in tiles, don't you?"

"Always," said Nora, grinning, and they walked on into the crowd.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Water in Every Corner
chapters.text:
A splashing sound pulled Nora toward a stone fountain shaped like a face. Water poured steadily from its open mouth.

"Where does all this water come from?" Nora asked, tracing a thin pipe along the wall with her finger.

"Follow it," said Tessera.

Nora followed the pipe down the street, past a bathhouse, past a second fountain, then a third. "There's water everywhere," she said.

"Pompeii had a clever water system," said Tessera. "**Lead pipes** carried water all through town, feeding public fountains so almost everyone could fill a jug nearby."

Nora cupped her hands under the stone mouth and let the water splash over her fingers, cool and clean. "No one had to carry water very far," she said. "That's actually kind of brilliant."

"People back then were not as simple as you might think," said Tessera.

Nora thought of her own bathroom tap at home, how she never once wondered where the water came from. "I'm never complaining about brushing my teeth again," she said.

"We'll see about that," said Tessera, nudging her toward the next street, where a low rumble of cheering drifted on the breeze.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Roaring Stone Circle
chapters.text:
The cheering grew louder. Nora turned a corner and gasped. A huge oval building rose above the rooftops, built entirely of stone.

"What IS that?" she asked.

"An **amphitheater**," said Tessera. "A big stone arena built for watching shows. This one was built around **70 BC** — one of the oldest ones we know of anywhere."

Nora counted the rows of seats circling upward, like rings inside a tree stump. "How many people fit in there?" she wondered aloud.

"Thousands," said Tessera. "People came to watch **gladiators** — performers who put on big, dramatic shows for roaring crowds."

Nora pictured the mosaic patterns in her kit at home, rows of tiles curving around a center. "It's built like a mosaic," she said. "Everything curving around one middle point."

"Never thought of it that way," said Tessera, "but you're right. Rings and rings, all fitting together."

A huge cheer rolled out from inside, so loud Nora felt it in her chest. She laughed instead of flinching.

"THAT'S LOUD!" she shouted, covering her ears and grinning at the same time.

"Wait till you hear what this whole mountain can do," said Tessera quietly, nodding toward a tall green shape in the distance.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Letters From Across the Bay
chapters.text:
Tessera carried Nora across the water, to a safe spot on the far side of the bay. "Watch, from here," Tessera said. "Stay close."

Nora looked back at Pompeii, small across the blue water. Everything felt calm, like any ordinary afternoon.

Then, on **August 24, in the year 79**, the mountain — Mount Vesuvius — let out a tremendous boom. A cloud shot into the sky, dark and enormous.

Nora's heart thumped. "Is it going to reach us?" she asked.

"No," said Tessera gently. "We're safe over here, watching from far away, just like someone real once did."

A young man nearby was scribbling fast on a scroll, eyes fixed on the cloud. "That's **Pliny the Younger**," said Tessera. "He wrote two whole letters describing exactly what he saw. He watched so carefully that scientists still call this kind of huge, fast eruption a **Plinian eruption**, named after him."

Nora watched him write. "He's basically taking notes," she said. "Like a reporter."

"Exactly like one," said Tessera. "And his uncle, Pliny the Elder, actually sailed his ships toward the danger that day, to help rescue people along the coast."

Nora's eyes went wide. "That's really brave."

"It was," said Tessera softly. "Not everyone ran away. Some people ran toward helping."

Nora watched the dark cloud a moment longer, then took a steady breath. "Okay," she said. "Show me what happened to the town."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Frozen in Ash
chapters.text:
Tessera brought Nora back, many quiet years later. The town was buried, covered by a thick blanket of grey.

"The ash and **pumice** — light, bubbly bits of volcanic rock — piled up **13 to 20 feet deep** over the whole town," said Tessera. "It happened fast enough to freeze everything in place."

Nora knelt by a half-dug doorway and peered inside. A loaf of bread sat in an oven, round and marked with lines, as if it had just come out that morning.

"It's still got the baker's stamp pressed into the top!" Nora gasped.

"IT'S STILL THERE!" she shouted, delighted.

"The ash kept it safe for almost two thousand years," said Tessera. "Paintings on walls survived too. Even writing people scratched into plaster survived."

Nora ran her fingers near a faded painting of leaves and birds, careful not to touch it. "It's like the whole town got paused," she said, "like someone hit pause on a game."

"That's exactly what happened," said Tessera. "One ordinary day, frozen, so people far in the future could walk through it."

Nora looked at the quiet street, the paused bread, the paused paintings. "I'm glad someone's finally unpausing it," she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Found Again
chapters.text:
Tessera tugged Nora forward through time once more, past centuries of quiet.

"In **1748**," said Tessera, "workers digging in this ground found old walls and broken statues poking up through the dirt. That's when people realized the whole town was still down here."

Nora watched shadowy figures with shovels, carefully brushing dirt from a mosaic floor. "They're being so gentle," she said.

"**Archaeologists** are people who dig up old things carefully, to learn about the past without breaking them," said Tessera. "They found Pompeii, and nearby, a smaller town called **Herculaneum**, buried by the same eruption, but under a different kind of material that kept even wooden furniture and old scrolls safe."

Nora peeked into a nearby villa. Painted walls covered every surface, deep red with mysterious figures mid-dance.

"That's called a **fresco** — a painting made right onto wet wall plaster," said Tessera. "This one's part of the famous Villa of the Mysteries. Nobody's fully sure what the painted scene even means."

Nora studied the shapes, the repeating poses. "It's a bit like my mosaic," she said. "Lots of little details, and you only see the whole story if you step back."

"That," said Tessera, "is exactly how history works too."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
"One more stop," said Tessera, and the light swirled Nora gently forward, all the way to today.

Crowds of visitors walked the same stepping-stone streets, cameras out, hats on against the sun. "People still come here?" Nora asked.

"Millions, every year," said Tessera. "Pompeii is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** now — a group that protects the world's most special places has promised to take extra good care of it."

Nora noticed roped-off sections, workers still gently brushing dirt from hidden floors. "Is there more to find?" she asked.

"A good part of the town is still waiting to be uncovered," said Tessera. "People keep finding new paintings, even now."

Nora looked up at the mountain beyond the rooftops, calm and green again. "Is it still... a volcano?" she asked carefully.

"It is," said Tessera. "**Still an active volcano**, and scientists watch it closely, because so many people live near it today."

Nora nodded slowly, then smiled. "I like that someone's always keeping an eye on it."

The light swirled once more, soft and warm, and Nora blinked — back on her bedroom carpet, her finished mosaic glowing gently beside her.

One new tessera sat on top of the pattern, a tiny deep red tile she didn't remember placing. She pressed it in. It fit perfectly.

"Every tiny piece tells a story," whispered Tessera, fading into the glass.

Nora smiled and pulled her blanket up.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Every tiny piece tells a story.

fact_pack.summary: Pompeii was a busy Roman town near the Bay of Naples that was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD. Ash and pumice covered the town so completely that it was preserved for almost 1,700 years, giving us an amazing snapshot of everyday Roman life.

facts.text: Pompeii was a Roman town in what is now southern Italy, near the modern city of Naples.
On August 24, 79 AD, the nearby volcano Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii in ash and pumice.
Before the eruption, Pompeii was a lively town of about 11,000 to 15,000 people with shops, bathhouses, theaters, and temples.
The eruption buried Pompeii under as much as 4 to 6 meters (13 to 20 feet) of volcanic ash and rock.
Many people in Pompeii escaped, but historians believe around 2,000 residents of the town died, with thousands more dying in nearby areas like Herculaneum.

A Roman writer named Pliny the Younger watched the eruption from across the bay and wrote two letters describing it in detail, which is why scientists call this kind of violent eruption a 'Plinian eruption'.
Pliny the Younger's uncle, Pliny the Elder, was a famous naval commander and author who sailed toward Pompeii to help people and died during the rescue attempt.
The eruption happened so fast that it froze the town in time, preserving bread in ovens, paintings on walls, and even graffiti on buildings.
Ash hardened around the bodies of victims, and later excavators poured plaster into the hollow spaces to make detailed casts showing their shapes and poses.
Pompeii was mostly forgotten for centuries until it was rediscovered in 1748, when workers digging in the area found ancient walls and artifacts.
Nearby Herculaneum, a smaller seaside town, was also buried by the same eruption but under a different kind of volcanic material that preserved even wooden furniture and scrolls.
Archaeologists have found colorful wall paintings called frescoes, including the famous 'Villa of the Mysteries' paintings showing mysterious rituals.
Pompeii had an advanced water system with public fountains and lead pipes bringing water throughout the town.
The town had a large amphitheater built around 70 BC, one of the oldest known Roman amphitheaters, used for gladiator games.
Archaeologists found a loaf of bread, still shaped and marked by its baker, preserved in a Pompeii oven.
A plaster cast of a dog, apparently chained and unable to escape, was found and is one of the most famous and sad discoveries from the site.
Pompeii's streets had raised stepping stones so people could cross without stepping in mud or water, while carts still passed through gaps in the stones.
Mount Vesuvius is still an active volcano today, and scientists continue to study and monitor it because millions of people live nearby.
Pompeii is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Italy's most visited archaeological parks, drawing millions of visitors each year.
Only about two-thirds of Pompeii has been excavated so far, and new discoveries, like freshly uncovered frescoes, are still being made.
Some buildings in Pompeii had advertisements and political slogans painted on their outside walls, an ancient form of public messaging.
The name 'Pompeii' likely comes from an ancient Oscan word 'pompe', meaning 'five', possibly referring to five original villages that joined together.

story.title: Ivy and the Rainbow Raindrop
story.subtitle: A splashy, colorful bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Jar
chapters.text:
Ivy sat on her bedroom floor, painting puddles after bedtime.

She dipped her brush in a jar of rainbow water. Drip, drip, drip went her brush.

Then the jar began to glow. A tiny light rose up and spun into a smiling drop.

"Hello, Ivy!" said the drop. "I'm Drip."

Ivy's eyes went wide. "A talking raindrop!"

Drip giggled. "Want to see how rainbows are made?"

Ivy grabbed her brush like a magic wand. "Yes, please!"

The jar swirled bright and pulled her right in.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Into the Raindrop
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! Ivy landed inside a giant, round raindrop.

Sunlight poured in through the top, bright and golden.

"Watch the light bend," said Drip.

The beam curved like one of Ivy's paintbrush lines.

Ivy traced the bend in the air with her finger.

"It bends just like my brush strokes!" she said.

Drip nodded. "Sunlight always bends a little when it goes into a drop, just like that."

Ivy clapped her hands. "I helped it bend!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Bouncy Back Wall
chapters.text:
BONK! The light hit the back wall of the drop.

It did not stop. It bounced right off, like a ball off a wall.

Ivy remembered bouncing her ball in her own bedroom.

"It's doing what my ball does!" she said.

Drip smiled. "The light bounces off the back, just like your bouncy ball."

Ivy bounced in place, copying the light's path.

"BOUNCE!" she shouted, and the light seemed to bounce even brighter.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Colors Come Out
chapters.text:
Now the light bent one more time, heading back out of the drop.

Suddenly, colors spilled everywhere: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple.

Ivy gasped. "Just like my paint tray!"

"White sunlight was hiding all those colors inside it, the whole time," said Drip.

Ivy pointed at each color, naming them from her own paints.

"Red, like my strawberry paint! Blue, like my puddle paint!"

Drip laughed. "You found every single color."

The colors swirled together into a little arc, right over Ivy's head.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Clever Old Thinker
chapters.text:
They floated to a cozy room full of books.

A kind man looked up and smiled at Ivy.

"I'm Ibn al-Haytham," he said. "I study how light moves."

Ivy tilted her head. "Like how it bent in the raindrop?"

"Just like that," he said. "Long, long ago, I watched light very closely."

Ivy showed him her bent paintbrush line from before.

He clapped softly. "You already understand it, Ivy."

Ivy beamed with pride.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Glass Ball Helper
chapters.text:
Next they met a man holding a big glass ball.

"I'm Kamal al-Din al-Farisi," he said. "This glass ball can act like a raindrop."

He filled it with water and shone sunlight through it.

Colors popped out the other side, just like before.

Ivy peeked into the glass ball. "It's like my jar!"

"Exactly," he said. "A little ball of water can show how raindrops make rainbows."

Ivy tapped her own jar happily, feeling very smart.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Newton's Magic Triangle
chapters.text:
A man with a glass triangle waved them over.

"I'm Isaac Newton," he said. "Watch this closely."

He held his glass triangle up to the sunlight.

Out came a stripe of every color, side by side by side.

Ivy's mouth made a little "oh."

"White light hides all those colors," Newton said. "My triangle just lets them out to play."

Ivy picked up an imaginary triangle and pretended to shine it too.

"I can do that too!" she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Sun Behind, Rain Ahead
chapters.text:
Drip led Ivy to a sunny puddle outside her own window.

"To see a rainbow," Drip said, "the sun must be behind you."

Ivy turned her back to the warm, bright sun.

"And rain needs to be out in front of you too," Drip added.

Ivy looked at the puddle, still sparkly from a little rain shower.

Suddenly, a real rainbow arched right over the puddle.

Ivy squealed with delight. "I made the rainbow rule work!"

Drip grinned. "Sun and rain together, that's the whole secret."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home Again
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! The jar glowed once more and set Ivy gently on her bedroom floor.

Her jar of paint water now had a tiny rainbow swirling inside it.

Drip waved from the water. "Goodnight, Ivy. You painted so well today."

Ivy yawned and hugged her soft blanket close.

She peeked at her rainbow jar one more sleepy time.

Outside her window, the real sky still held a soft, fading rainbow.

Ivy closed her eyes, dreaming in every color she knew.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ivy. Paint bright, dream bright.

The rain needs to be out in front of you too.

fact_pack.summary: Rainbows appear when sunlight passes through raindrops and gets bent, split into colors, and bounced back to our eyes. They are a science-and-wonder topic: a physics lesson dressed up as a beautiful arc in the sky, with plenty of fun details for kids to explore.

facts.text: A rainbow forms when sunlight enters a raindrop, bends, reflects off the inside back of the drop, and bends again as it exits.
This bending of light is called refraction, and it happens because light slows down and changes direction when it moves from air into water.
White sunlight is actually made of many colors mixed together, and raindrops separate them because each color bends by a slightly different amount.
The classic rainbow color order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet, often remembered with the name 'Roy G. Biv'.
Red always appears on the outer edge of a rainbow and violet on the inner edge because red bends the least and violet bends the most.
To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and rain (or spray) must be in front of you.
Rainbows are actually full circles, but we usually only see an arc because the ground blocks the bottom half.
From an airplane, people sometimes see a complete circular rainbow because there is no ground in the way.
Every person actually sees a slightly different rainbow, made from different raindrops, because the angle of light to your eyes is unique to your position.
A rainbow always appears in the part of the sky directly opposite the sun, centered on a point called the antisolar point.
Sometimes a fainter second rainbow appears above the main one, with its colors reversed, caused by light bouncing twice inside the raindrops.
The dark strip of sky between a primary and secondary rainbow is called Alexander's band, named after the ancient Greek philosopher Alexander of Aphrodisias who described it around 200 AD.
Rainbows can also form in mist, waterfalls, garden hose spray, and even moonlight, where they are called moonbows.
Moonbows are usually so faint that they look white or gray to human eyes, though cameras can capture their colors.
The scientist Isaac Newton showed in the 1660s that a glass prism could split white light into the same rainbow of colors, proving light itself contains all the colors.
The Persian scientist Ibn al-Haytham and later Kamal al-Din al-Farisi studied light and rainbows in raindrops centuries before Newton, around the 1000s and 1300s.
Many cultures have myths about rainbows, such as the Norse story of Bifrost, a rainbow bridge connecting Earth to the home of the gods.
In the Bible, the rainbow appears as a sign of a promise from God to Noah after a great flood.
Many cultures tell of a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow, especially in Irish folklore involving leprechauns, though a rainbow's end is never a real fixed spot since it moves as you move.
Because a rainbow depends on where the viewer stands, you can never actually walk up to or touch one.
Rainbows need both sunlight and water droplets at the same time, which is why they often appear during or right after a rain shower when the sun peeks out.
A rainbow's size in the sky is always about the same, spanning roughly 42 degrees from the antisolar point for the primary bow.
The rainbow flag, created by artist Gilbert Baker in 1978, uses rainbow colors as a symbol of pride and diversity.
Rainbows are studied in a branch of science called optics, which explores how light behaves, bends, and reflects.

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Brick Full of Sharks
story.subtitle: A splashy swim through the history of sharks

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Glows Again
chapters.text:
Milo snapped a LEGO shark fin onto his tower. Juno stomped her toy dinosaur across the rug, roaring.

It had been one whole week since their giant tower went **CLICK** and held.

Now the top brick began to glow. Soft and red.

"It's doing the thing again!" Milo whispered.

Juno dropped her dinosaur. "Brick magic!"

The brick clicked three times. The carpet rippled like water. **WHOOOOSH!** The bedroom spun into blue.

Milo and Juno landed with a soft splash on sand under the sea.

A round gray shark with a kind eye swam up close. "Hello! I'm Finn. I show kids around the ocean."

"Are you gonna eat us?" Juno asked, grabbing Milo's hand.

Finn laughed, little bubbles popping. "No way. I just want to show you my friends."

Milo grinned. "Sharks! I KNEW this brick liked sharks."

"Sharks aren't like other fish," said Finn. "Their bones are soft and bendy. Bendy like the squishy part of your ear. Not hard like yours."

Juno poked her own ear. "Squishy!"

"And there are more than **500 kinds** of sharks swimming around today," Finn said.

Milo counted on his fingers and gave up fast. "That's SO many."

"Follow me," said Finn. "I'll show you the biggest one first."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A huge shadow slid over them. Juno gasped and grabbed Milo's arm.

"Is that a whale?" Milo asked.

"Nope!" said Finn. "That's a **whale shark**. The biggest fish in the whole world."

The giant shark swam closer. Its mouth hung open like a cave.

Juno squeaked. "It's gonna eat us!"

Finn chuckled. "Don't worry. It only eats tiny floating bits called plankton. Little drifting dots of food, smaller than your fingernail."

The whale shark swooshed by. Its mouth strained the water like a big sieve.

Milo watched close. "It's HUGE. But it only eats tiny snacks?"

"Over **40 feet** long," Finn said. "And yes. Tiny snacks."

Juno waved at the giant fish. "Bye, gentle giant!"

The whale shark gave a slow, friendly flick of its tail and swam on.

"That wasn't scary at all," Juno said. She let go of Milo's arm.

"Nope," said Milo. "It's just a big, gentle vacuum cleaner."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Smile Full of Teeth
chapters.text:
Milo's eyes went wide. "Whoa. Triangle teeth!"

A sleek shark glided by. Its teeth looked like little white triangles, lined up in rows.

"That's a **great white shark**," said Finn. "It can grow up to **20 feet** long."

Juno counted the teeth from a safe distance. "One, two, three. So many!"

"Sharks lose teeth all the time," Finn said. "But new ones keep moving up to take their place. **Thousands** in one shark's whole life!"

Milo grinned. "Like a never-ending teeth factory!"

"Exactly," said Finn.

The great white swam in a slow circle. It didn't even look at the kids. Then it turned and vanished into the blue.

"It didn't even look at us," Milo noticed.

"Sharks aren't looking for kids to munch," Finn said. "They'd rather find fish."

Juno patted her own tooth, wiggly from losing one. "I only get ONE new tooth. Lucky shark."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Giant From Long Ago
chapters.text:
Juno dug her toes into the sand and gasped. "A TOOTH! Bigger than my hand!"

She held up a giant triangle tooth. It was as big as her whole palm.

"That belonged to **Megalodon**," Finn said. "The biggest shark that ever lived."

Milo's mouth dropped open. "Bigger than the great white?"

"Way bigger," said Finn. "But Megalodon is extinct now. That means none are swimming anywhere today. They all disappeared a long, long time ago."

Juno hugged the giant tooth like a treasure. "Just like my dinosaurs!"

"Exactly like your dinosaurs," said Finn. "We mostly know about Megalodon from its teeth. They turned into stone over time. We call that a fossil."

Milo tapped the tooth gently. "So this rock used to be a real tooth?"

"It sure did," said Finn.

Juno held the tooth up high. "I'm keeping this old giant in my memory forever!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sandpaper Skin and Sparkle Spots
chapters.text:
"Can I touch your skin?" Milo asked.

"Go ahead," said Finn.

Milo patted him gently. "Whoa, it's like sandpaper!"

"My skin is covered in tiny tooth-shaped bumps," Finn said. "They help me zoom through the water extra smooth."

Juno patted too, careful and slow. "Bumpy but smooth!"

"Look at my nose," said Finn. He pointed to tiny dots near his snout. "Those are special jelly spots. They feel tiny sparks from other animals swimming nearby. Even in the dark."

Milo's eyes lit up. "So you can feel someone without even seeing them?"

"Yep," said Finn. "Like a secret shark superpower."

Juno waved her hand near Finn's nose. "Do you feel me?"

Finn's nose twitched. "I feel a little spark of Juno!"

Juno giggled so hard she almost fell off a rock.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Walking, Hammers, and Speed
chapters.text:
"Look!" Milo pointed. "That shark is... WALKING?"

A small spotted shark flip-flopped across the coral. It used its fins like little paddles.

"That's an **epaulette shark**," Finn said. "It can walk across reefs. It barely needs much air to do it for hours."

Juno stomped her feet like the shark. "I'm walking too!"

A strange shadow passed above them. A shark with a head shaped like a hammer.

"Whoa, its head is so WIDE," Milo said.

"That's a **hammerhead**," said Finn. "Its wide head spreads its eyes far apart. It helps the shark see almost all the way around."

Juno spun in a circle. "Like watching in every direction!"

Then something zipped by in a blink. "What was THAT?" Milo gasped.

"The **shortfin mako**," Finn said. "Fastest shark in the sea. Here one second, gone the next."

Juno clapped both hands. "ZOOM!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Purses, Rivers, and Resting Spots
chapters.text:
Milo found a curly brown pouch stuck to a plant. "What's this weird pocket?"

"That's called a mermaid's purse," said Finn. "Some baby sharks hatch out of cases like that one. Other sharks just have live babies that swim right out, ready to go."

Juno peeked inside, careful not to touch. "Baby shark in a pocket!"

"Some sharks even swim up rivers," Finn said. "**Bull sharks** can live in salty ocean water and in fresh river water too. They've been found swimming far, far upstream."

Milo blinked. "Sharks... in a river?"

"Yep," said Finn.

Down on the sandy floor, a shark lay very still. Water pumped gently over its gills. Gills are the parts fish use to breathe underwater, like we use our lungs.

"Is it sleeping?" Juno whispered.

"Resting," Finn said. "**Nurse sharks** can rest right on the bottom and still breathe just fine."

"Sharks keep the whole ocean balanced too," Finn added. "They help keep other animals in check. Like a good team captain."

Milo nodded slowly. "Sharks do a LOT of jobs."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady and the Way Home
chapters.text:
Finn led them to a quiet cove. A shimmer in the water showed a smiling woman swimming beside sharks.

"That's **Eugenie Clark**," Finn said. "People called her the Shark Lady. She studied sharks for years and years. She showed that sharks are curious. Some can even learn tricks, like puppies."

Juno gasped. "Sharks do TRICKS?"

"Some can," said Finn, smiling.

"How long do sharks even live?" Milo asked.

"Some whale sharks might live past **100 years**," Finn said. "Longer than almost any other fish."

Juno yawned a giant yawn. "That's older than Grandpa!"

Finn chuckled. "Time to go home, I think."

The glowing red brick floated up from the sand, clicking softly.

"Bye, Finn!" Milo waved.

"Play well," Finn called back. "And swim well too!"

**WHOOOOSH!** The ocean spun away into bedroom carpet.

Milo and Juno landed softly by their LEGO tower. On top sat one new brick, shaped like a tiny shark tooth. It glowed once, then went still.

Juno hugged her dinosaur tight. "Best. Trip. Ever."

Milo smiled at the tower. "Goodnight, ocean. Goodnight, sharks."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

story.title: Lena and the Keeper's Glove
story.subtitle: A goalkeeper's glove, a green door, and two thousand years of goals.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Hum in the Closet
chapters.text:
Lena was supposed to be asleep an hour ago.

Instead she was belly-down on her carpet, diving sideways to catch a balled-up sock before it hit her pillow. Goalkeeping practice didn't stop for bedtime.

Reaching under her bed for the sock, her hand closed on something stiff and cracked instead — an old leather glove, far too big for her hand, humming faintly green.

The second she pulled it on, the hum became a voice. "Finally," it said. "A keeper who dives."

A doorway opened in her closet, shaped exactly like a goalmouth, glowing green at the edges.

"Who—"

"Call me Keeper," said the glove. "Step through. There's two thousand years of goals to see."

Lena laughed and stepped into the light.

She landed in a dusty courtyard in **ancient China**, where men in long tunics kicked a leather ball through a small hoop strung between two poles.

"This is **cuju**," Keeper said. "People here were kicking a ball like this more than **2,000 years ago** — one of soccer's oldest known ancestors."

A wild kick sailed wide. Lena's goalkeeper instincts fired before she could think, and she snagged the ball out of the air. The players froze, then bowed, grinning.

Lena bowed back. "Best save tonight. And it's only chapter one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Banned in London
chapters.text:
Keeper tugged her through swirling fog into a narrow street packed with yelling men, all chasing one ball toward nowhere in particular.

"Watch your toes," Keeper said. "This is **mob football** — medieval England's version of soccer. No field, no teams, barely any rules."

A man scooped the ball up and sprinted off with it tucked under his arm. Lena winced. "Wait — hands? That's not soccer."

"Not yet," Keeper said. "Carrying the ball was normal for centuries. So normal, in fact, it got too wild — **King Edward II banned it in London in 1314** for causing trouble in the streets."

"Somebody better fix this," Lena muttered, dodging a runner. "Watching people carry the ball around is driving me crazy."

Keeper chuckled. "Funny you say that. Centuries later, schoolboys called their no-hands version '**assoc**,' short for association football. By the **1880s**, that got shortened again — to '**soccer**.'"

"Finally," Lena said. "A name I recognize."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Rulebook
chapters.text:
Keeper dropped her into a smoky London room in **1863**, where a dozen serious men argued around a table covered in papers.

"They're trying to agree on one rulebook," Keeper said. "Cambridge University students tried first, back in **1848**, with the **Cambridge Rules**. It didn't stick everywhere."

One man kept insisting players should carry the ball and run. Lena, arms crossed, had heard this argument three times already.

"If you let people carry it," she said, loud enough for the table to hear, "it's not even the same game as kicking it. Pick one."

The room went quiet. A tall man with excellent sideburns turned, surprised, then nodded and wrote something down.

"That's **Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Keeper whispered. "Founder of **The Football Association**, started right here on **26 October, 1863**. He's about to write football's first official Laws of the Game — carrying the ball by hand, banned for good."

Lena grinned. "I didn't do that."

"Sure you didn't," said Keeper.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Glasgow, 1872
chapters.text:
Fog rolled across a muddy field. Boots squelched, and a crowd murmured with every near-miss.

"Welcome to Glasgow," Keeper said. "This is the first-ever **official international match** — Scotland versus England, **1872**. Before this, there's already the **FA Cup**, started in **1871** — still the oldest football competition running anywhere in the world."

A Scotland forward's shot skimmed the crossbar. The goalkeeper dove sideways and barely got a hand to it.

"That keeper's good," Lena said, impressed.

Shot after shot, save after save, neither side budged. Lena studied both keepers' footwork, nodding slowly.

"Nobody's scoring today," she said finally. "This one's ending nil-nil."

Keeper smiled. "Good read. It finished **0–0**."

"Two great keepers," Lena said, "and not one goal. That's basically my dream match."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Leagues and a World Office
chapters.text:
Keeper set her down beside a noisy train platform in **1888**, where a man scribbled furiously, surrounded by confused team captains.

"That's **William McGregor**," Keeper said. "Teams keep showing up on the wrong days, playing whoever's free."

Lena peered at the chaos. "You need a schedule," she said. "Every team in one list, everybody plays everybody, keep count of wins."

McGregor looked up, startled, then grinned and started drawing a table.

"That became the **Football League**," Keeper said, "the world's first, in **1888**."

Before Lena could celebrate, Keeper tugged her into an office in **Paris**, lined with flags.

"Different problem," Keeper said. "Countries all play now, but nobody agrees whose rules count internationally."

"So make one office for the whole world," Lena said.

"Exactly what seven countries decided in **1904**," Keeper said, "when they founded **FIFA** right here."

Lena looked at the flags. "Soccer's everywhere now."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Oldest Ball in the World
chapters.text:
Keeper led her up a spiral staircase inside a cold stone castle, dust drifting in beams of light.

"**Stirling Castle**, Scotland," Keeper said. "Eyes on the rafters."

Old wood creaked above, and a lumpy shape tumbled loose. Lena dove, glove outstretched, and caught it an inch from the floor.

"Careful," Keeper said, as Lena sat up cradling a soft, leather-wrapped ball. "You might be holding the **oldest football in the world**."

"This old thing?"

"Found hidden right here — might date back to the **1540s**. Nobody's totally sure, that part's a bit of a guess — but if it's right, people have been kicking a ball around a very long time."

Lena held it up like a trophy. "Good thing somebody's reflexes were paying attention."

"Lucky catch," Keeper agreed. "Literally saved history."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Ban That Should Never Have Been
chapters.text:
A roar hit Lena the moment the doorway opened — a packed stadium, thousands on their feet.

"Who's playing?" she shouted.

"The **Dick, Kerr Ladies**," Keeper said, "one of England's most popular teams, thanks mostly to star forward **Lily Parr**."

Parr curled a shot past the goalkeeper, and the stadium exploded. "She's incredible," Lena said. "Why haven't I heard of her?"

Keeper's voice flattened. "Because in **1921**, the Football Association banned women's football in England completely."

Lena's jaw dropped. "That's not fair. She's clearly better than half the men I've seen tonight."

"You're right," Keeper said. "It took **fifty years** — until **1971** — for the FA to finally lift that ban."

"Fifty years," Lena repeated, shaking her head. "Too long."

"Here's the good part." The scene shifted to a stadium in **China**. "**1991**, the first official **Women's World Cup**. Winner: the **United States**."

Lena pumped her fist. "About time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The First World Cup
chapters.text:
The next doorway dropped Lena into a roaring stadium in **Uruguay**, **1930**.

"First-ever **FIFA World Cup**," Keeper said. "**Jules Rimet's** idea — he's FIFA's president, pushing to get every country's best team together."

"Who's in the final?" Lena asked.

"Host country Uruguay, against Argentina."

The whistle blew. Uruguay attacked in waves, and when the final goal went in, the home crowd lost their minds, flags waving everywhere.

"Uruguay wins the very first World Cup," Keeper said over the noise.

A shiny statue got carried out on a cushion. "What's that?"

"The trophy," Keeper said. "Named the **Jules Rimet Trophy**, after the man who made this whole tournament happen."

Lena watched it glint. "So it all started right here."

"And it only gets weirder," Keeper said, already reaching for the next doorway.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Trophies, Dogs, and Cards
chapters.text:
London, **1966**. Lena landed beside a very worried crowd outside a building.

"They've lost the actual World Cup trophy," Keeper said. "Stolen, right off display."

"Did they find it?"

"A week later," Keeper said, "a dog named **Pickles** sniffed it out, wrapped in newspaper, under a hedge."

Lena laughed. "A dog saved the World Cup?"

"That same year, **England hosted the tournament — and won it**. Still their only title." Keeper tugged her through a blur of stadiums. "Brazil's collected titles too — **five**: **1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002**."

"That's a lot," Lena said.

"One player was on three of those winning teams," Keeper said. "**Pele** — **1958, 1962, and 1970**. Nobody's matched that since."

A referee marched onto a field, holding up something small and bright. "What's that?"

"**Ken Aston**," Keeper said. "He just invented **yellow and red cards**, inspired by traffic lights, debuting at that **1970 World Cup**."

"Stop, go," Lena said. "Makes sense."

"One more thing," Keeper added. "Brazil kept that original trophy for good after their third win, so FIFA made a **new trophy in 1974**. Still the one teams lift today."

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The doorway spat Lena right back onto her bedroom carpet, sock-ball still lying where she'd left it.

The glove had gone quiet in her hand, just old cracked leather again.

"Same time tomorrow?" she whispered.

Nothing hummed back — but when she set the glove down, she noticed something new on her windowsill: a small, lumpy leather ball, soft stitches and all, just like the one from Stirling Castle.

Lena grinned, pulled up her blanket, and glanced at the clock. Way too late. Worth every minute.

She had a scrimmage after school tomorrow, and for the first time ever, she couldn't wait to go in goal.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow's scrimmage didn't stand a chance.
