story.title: Theo and the Game That Never Stopped
story.subtitle: A Roblox-powered kickabout through 2,000 years of soccer.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Kick Heard for 2,000 Years (Han China)
chapters.text:
Theo had been awake for one more level than he should have.

His laptop glowed on the carpet, Roblox Studio open, a half-finished penalty-kick game loading in the corner. Last night's message still sat burned into his memory: THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD. Tonight he was only testing the ball's bounce.

He typed one more line of code. It blinked green instead of white.

The whole screen flickered, black then green then black again. A tiny green figure snapped into focus, eight blocky pixels tall, squeaking like an old modem with opinions.

"PLAYER ONE," said Bit. "Ready for tonight's build?"

"You're back," Theo said, grinning. "Please tell me this one has a trophy."

"BZZZT. Every level does. One golden coin each. Save enough levels, they fuse into something shiny at the end." Bit's pixels rearranged into a dusty field under a pale sun. "Welcome to **Han China**, more than **2,000 years ago**."

Men in long tunics chased a round leather ball across packed dirt, using only their feet, never their hands.

"That's basically what I do at practice," Theo said. "No hands. Just feet, knees, head."

"BZZZT. Correct. This game is called **Cuju**. It's one of the oldest known kicking games on Earth. Some people call it soccer's great-great-great-grandparent."

Theo watched a kid his own age flub a pass, get laughed at, and immediately try again. Some things, apparently, never changed.

"If this is the first level," Theo said, "the rule has to be no hands. That's the whole point. I'm putting that in my game tonight."

"A rule written down becomes a rule that lasts," Bit said. "BZZZT. **Level complete.**"

A golden coin spun out of nowhere and landed in Theo's palm, cold and bright.

"One down," Bit said. "Shall we go further back — I mean forward? Time's weird in here."

Theo laughed and pocketed the coin. "Let's go."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Wildest Game in England (1314)
chapters.text:
The ground shook before Theo saw why.

A roaring crowd of grown men came pelting down a muddy street, kicking, shoving, and occasionally tackling each other into a fence. Somewhere in the middle of it all was a ball.

"Meet **mob football**," Bit said, hovering well out of the way. "Whole villages against whole villages. No fixed field. No fixed rules. Sometimes you just... start."

"That looks less like a sport and more like a traffic jam with legs," Theo said, ducking a flying elbow.

"BZZZT. **King Edward II** agreed. He banned the game in **London** in **1314**. Said it was too wild for the streets."

Theo spotted something half-buried near a stone wall: an old, round, stitched-leather ball, flattened with age. He picked it up. It was lighter than it looked, and lumpy.

"What's inside this thing?"

"Go on, guess, Player One."

Theo squeezed it. Something soft shifted under the leather. "Not air. Feels like an actual squishy bit."

"BZZZT. Close enough. Old footballs like this one were stuffed with an inflated **pig's bladder** — basically nature's balloon. A ball just like this one turned up hidden at **Stirling Castle** in Scotland. People think it might date back to the **1540s**. If so, it's the oldest football in the world."

Theo turned the ball over in his hands. It looked exactly like something a kid would've kicked around and then forgotten for five hundred years.

"No wonder they banned it," Theo said. "People needed actual rules before somebody got hurt."

"BZZZT. Rules were coming. Eventually. It only took about **five hundred years**."

Another coin dropped, landing next to the first with a tiny clink.

"Progress," Theo said, "is slow."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Rulebook Wars (1848–1863)
chapters.text:
The scene changed to a wood-paneled room full of serious young men arguing over a chalkboard.

"**Cambridge University**, **1848**," Bit announced. "Students from different schools, all taught football differently, trying to agree on one rulebook. Spoiler: it did not go smoothly."

One student insisted players should be allowed to catch the ball and run with it. Another insisted that was basically cheating.

"Sounds like my Discord," Theo muttered. "Somebody always wants to carry the ball."

"BZZZT. Fifteen years later, it got worse before it got better."

The scene shifted: a London room, **1863**, men founding something called the **Football Association**, the FA. At the head of the table sat a serious man with excellent handwriting.

"That's **Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Bit said. "He personally wrote football's first official rulebook, called the **Laws of the Game**."

Theo leaned over his shoulder, reading upside down. "You still haven't fixed the hands problem."

Morley looked up, startled.

"Pick one," Theo said. "Either it's a kicking game or a carrying game. You can't have both or nobody will ever agree on anything."

Morley considered this a long moment. Then he dipped his pen and wrote something down.

"BZZZT," Bit whispered. "He just banned carrying the ball by hand. Forever. That's actually the rule, Theo."

Theo stared at the page. "I did that?"

"Let's say you had excellent timing."

A third coin landed in his palm, and somewhere outside, a bell rang like a very old notification sound.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Oldest Cup, The Flattest Draw (1871–1872)
chapters.text:
A trophy cabinet appeared out of the pixel fog, empty except for one shiny cup with a dent in the lid.

"The **FA Cup**," Bit said. "First played in **1871 and 1872**. Still running today. Oldest football competition on the planet."

"Older than my Roblox game?" Theo asked.

"BZZZT. Considerably."

The scene shifted to a foggy field in **Glasgow**, lined with spectators in hats. A sign read SCOTLAND vs ENGLAND, **1872** — the very first official international match ever played.

"Big game," Theo said, rubbing his hands the way he always did before a penalty. "Who won?"

"Guess."

Both sides looked nervous, careful, like nobody wanted to make the mistake.

"Based on how stressed everyone looks," Theo said, "nobody scores. I say nothing to nothing."

The final whistle blew. The scoreboard stayed exactly as it started: 0–0.

"BZZZT. Correct. First international match in history. A scoreless draw."

Theo threw his hands up. "A hundred and fifty years, and the first big game ever was a snoozer? Some things never change."

"To be fair," Bit said, "nobody had invented penalty kicks yet. Give it time."

"Don't tempt me," Theo muttered, already itching for one.

He pocketed the fourth coin, warm from the last three.

chapters.heading: Level 5: One Game, One World (1888–1904)
chapters.text:
A scoreboard the size of a wall lit up, covered in team names and columns of numbers.

"**1888**," Bit said. "A man named **William McGregor** had an idea: instead of teams challenging each other whenever they felt like it, why not make everyone play everyone else across a whole season, keeping score the whole way?"

Theo's eyes went wide. "That's a league table. That's literally what I built for my game's season mode."

"BZZZT. Correct. The **Football League** — the first one anywhere in the world."

Nearby, a chalk shop sign read FOOTBALL — or ASSOC., for short.

Theo squinted at it. "Assoc of what?"

"Association football. Its full name. Around the **1880s**, English schoolboys started shortening 'assoc' into a nickname."

Theo tried it out loud. "Assoc... assocker... soccer." He laughed. "That's where 'soccer' comes from?"

"BZZZT. That's where 'soccer' comes from."

The scene shifted to a grand room in **Paris**, where people from seven different countries sat down together in **1904** to found something new.

"**FIFA**," Bit said. "The group that makes sure football follows the same rules everywhere on Earth."

"Good," Theo said. "My multiplayer game breaks instantly if even one player's got different rules than everyone else."

"BZZZT. You and FIFA, same headache, seventy years apart."

Coin number five dropped. Theo was starting to need bigger pockets.

chapters.heading: Level 6: The First World Cup (Uruguay, 1930)
chapters.text:
The air itself seemed to roar.

Theo landed in a packed stadium, flags waving, noise rolling down from the stands. Two teams in bright colors lined up for a final.

"**1930**," Bit said. "The very first **FIFA World Cup**, hosted by **Uruguay**. One tournament, the best teams from everywhere, all fighting for one trophy — the whole idea came from a FIFA president named **Jules Rimet**."

A small gold statue sat on a nearby table, a figure holding a ball overhead.

"Let me guess," Theo said. "Named after—"

"BZZZT. The **Jules Rimet Trophy**. Got it in one."

Theo watched Uruguay surge forward, the home crowd rising with every attack.

"Home team's got the whole stadium screaming for them," Theo said. "That's basically an extra player."

"BZZZT. Maybe that's why **Uruguay beat Argentina** in the final, right here, in front of their own fans."

The whistle blew and the stadium erupted, hats flying, strangers hugging strangers.

"Imagine building a whole game," Theo said, "and then watching the entire world show up to play it."

"That," Bit said, "is more or less what you're doing every night at your laptop. Just smaller crowds. So far."

Theo rolled his eyes, still smiling as coin number six dropped into his hand.

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Dog Who Saved the World Cup (1966)
chapters.text:
A newspaper spun through the air and landed flat at Theo's feet. The headline read: WORLD CUP STOLEN!

"**1966**," Bit said. "The actual **World Cup trophy** vanished right out from under everyone's nose, in **London**, days before the tournament."

Theo's jaw dropped. "Someone just took it?"

"BZZZT. Gone. Nobody could find it anywhere."

"So how'd they get it back?"

Theo thought of his own dog, who could find a dropped chicken nugget from two rooms away using nothing but a very good nose.

"A dog," Theo said slowly. "You need a dog. Noses beat eyeballs every time."

"BZZZT. **A dog named Pickles** found the missing trophy safe, one week later. Sniffed it right out."

"I KNEW it," Theo said, pumping a fist. "Good boy, Pickles."

With the trophy back where it belonged, the tournament went ahead. The scene shifted to a roaring stadium, and **England**, playing as host, lifted the cup at the end of it.

"Their only World Cup win so far," Bit added. "**1966**. Still talked about constantly, to this day."

"Good for them," Theo said. "After the dog saved the whole tournament, somebody had to win it."

Coin seven landed with a satisfying clink.

chapters.heading: Level 8: Pele, the Traffic Light, and the New Trophy (1958–1974)
chapters.text:
Five golden trophies floated in the pixel haze, each stamped with a different year.

"**Brazil**," Bit said. "Five World Cup wins. **1958, 1962, 1970, 1994**, and **2002**. Nobody else has won more."

Theo whistled. "And let me guess, one guy's on half of those."

"BZZZT. One player — **Pele** — played on **three** of Brazil's winning squads: **1958, 1962**, and **1970**. The only player in history to manage that."

Theo watched grainy footage of a young Pele weaving through defenders like they weren't there.

"What's that about?" He pointed at a referee holding up two small cards, one yellow, one red.

"That's **Ken Aston**, a referee. He got the idea from a traffic light. Green means go, yellow means slow down and be careful, red means stop completely."

"So yellow's a warning," Theo said, "and red means you're out."

"BZZZT. Debuted at the **1970 World Cup**. Before that, referees just sort of... shouted."

"I did this exact thing for my game's foul system," Theo said. "Green, you're fine. Yellow, chill out. Red, benched."

"BZZZT. You and Ken Aston, same brainwave, fifty-some years apart."

One more trophy floated closer, shinier, clearly brand new.

"After Brazil's third win, they got to keep the original trophy forever," Bit explained. "So in **1974**, FIFA had to make a whole new one."

"They won so hard they broke the trophy system," Theo said. "Incredible."

Coin number eight landed, heavier than the rest, somehow.

chapters.heading: Level 9: The Game They Tried to Ban (1921–1991)
chapters.text:
A packed stadium appeared again, except this time every player on the field was a woman.

"Meet the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**," Bit said. "One of the most popular football teams in all of England, thanks largely to a forward named **Lily Parr**."

Theo watched Lily Parr blast a shot past a goalkeeper who never had a chance.

"She's incredible," Theo said. "Why haven't I heard of her?"

Bit's voice dropped, just slightly. "Because in **1921**, the FA banned women's football completely. It simply wasn't fair, Theo. Women who loved the game and were brilliant at it weren't allowed to play it on proper grounds anymore."

Theo frowned, genuinely annoyed on her behalf. "That's ridiculous. She was clearly better than half the guys out there."

"BZZZT. Agreed completely. But here's the good part: the ban didn't last forever. It got lifted in **1971**, fifty years after it started."

The scene shifted to a sunlit stadium in **China**, banners everywhere, crowds roaring.

"**1991**," Bit said. "The very first official **Women's World Cup**. Won by the **United States**."

Theo grinned. "So the game came back even bigger."

"BZZZT. Much bigger."

"My team's got girls who could outplay basically anyone," Theo said. "I'm adding a women's league to my game tonight. Lily Parr gets a jersey in my code. Non-negotiable."

Bit's pixel eyes glowed warm and bright. "**Level complete.**"

The ninth coin dropped, shaped, for just a second, like a tiny trophy already.

chapters.heading: Full Time
chapters.text:
The pixel fog thinned, and Theo's bedroom carpet solidified under his knees.

His laptop sat exactly where he'd left it, cursor blinking patiently in his half-built game.

Nine golden coins sat in a neat row on the carpet, each one warm, each one real.

"Go on," Bit said, hovering by the screen, voice smaller than usual. "You know how this part works."

Theo nudged the coins together. They slid toward each other, melted into light, and reformed into a small golden trophy, dented slightly on one side, exactly like the one from 1930.

"Every level you saved tonight," Bit said, "from a dusty field in China to a dog named Pickles, built the game you're about to make. **2,000 years** of people arguing about one ball, Theo. And you get to add the next bit."

Theo turned the little trophy over in his hands. "No pressure."

"BZZZT. All the pressure. That's the fun part."

Bit's pixel eyes flickered, bright and a little watery, the way they always did right before a level ended for good.

"**Player One**," Bit said softly. "**Level complete.**"

The screen dimmed to black, then to Theo's ordinary desktop, cursor still blinking in his game file.

Theo set the little trophy on his shelf, next to nothing else yet, but clearly meant for company.

There was a whole foul system to code, a women's league to build, and one very good dog to put in a cutscene somewhere.

He closed the laptop and went to bed, grinning.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a whole league left to build.

story.title: Mia and the Whistle That Remembers Everything
story.subtitle: A ninety-minute tour through the history of the world's biggest game

chapters.heading: Minute 1: Kick-Off in Han China
chapters.text:
Mia had the spreadsheet open at 11:47 p.m., which was against every rule her mother had ever made about school nights.

She was building her own version of expected goals — the stat that scores a shot not on whether it went in, but on how good a chance it really was. Her team had lost two-nil that afternoon, and she was convinced the numbers would prove they'd actually been unlucky.

Her laptop screen flickered green. The columns of numbers scrolled sideways, then folded into a shape she recognized instantly: a soccer pitch, lines and all.

On her desk, the brass whistle her grandfather had given her — the one he'd blown for forty years of Saturday matches — started to hum.

"Statistically speaking," said a voice, "you are up well past your bedtime."

The whistle was talking. Or rather, something made of light now stood where the whistle had been, shaped roughly like a referee if a referee were drawn entirely out of glowing chalk lines.

"I'm Pip," it said. "I officiate history. Would you like to see the opening kickoff? The *real* one?"

Before Mia could ask what that meant, the floor dropped away like a missed tackle, and she landed in warm sunlight, in a dusty yard full of shouting men in silk tunics, kicking a leather ball between two bamboo poles.

"Where—" Mia started.

"**Han China**," Pip said. "A little over **2,000 years ago**. This game is called ***cuju*** — roughly 'kickball.' One of the oldest known relatives of the sport you watch on Saturdays."

Mia watched a player flick the ball up with his heel, juggle it twice, then thread it between the poles without ever using his hands. The crowd roared.

"That's not luck," Mia said slowly, tracking the arc of the ball. "His first touch set the whole angle up. He basically pre-loaded that shot three moves early."

"Go on," said Pip, sounding entertained.

"It's like my model," Mia said. "You don't judge the goal. You judge the decisions that built it."

Pip's chalk-outline face did something that might have been a grin. "Two thousand years, and a teenager on a Tuesday night just explained cuju better than most commentators. Welcome to the pitch, Mia. Try not to get sent off."

chapters.heading: Minute 15: The Game a King Banned
chapters.text:
Pip blew a short note on an invisible whistle, and the dusty yard dissolved into mud, fog, and a great deal more shouting.

Mia stumbled into what looked like an entire village at war with itself. Dozens of men were dragging a leather ball down a muddy street, through a hedge, past a church, and apparently straight through someone's front garden.

"This is still soccer?" Mia said, dodging an elbow.

"Loosely," said Pip. "**Medieval England** — this is 'mob football.' No set number of players, barely any rules, and the goal might be a mile away in the next village. It got so out of hand that **King Edward the Second banned it in London in 1314**, worried it was causing riots in the streets."

Mia watched two men collide shoulder-first into a cart, which tipped over, spilling cabbages everywhere. Nobody stopped playing.

"I can see why," she said, stepping over a rolling cabbage.

Pip steered her sideways, through what felt like a wall of fog, into a cooler, quieter stone room. A castle room. On a dusty shelf sat a shriveled, leathery lump she only recognized as a ball because of its shape.

"Found hidden at **Stirling Castle, in Scotland**," Pip said. "Might date back to the **1540s** — which would make it the oldest football in the world. It's made from a pig's bladder, laced inside a leather case."

Mia leaned in. "Wait — so for most of history, the ball itself was basically something you'd compost?"

"Mostly air and old animal parts, yes," said Pip. "Try not to think about it too hard during half-time snacks."

Mia laughed despite herself, then noticed something: a tally of wins scratched into the stone beside the ball, worn smooth by centuries of thumbs.

"Somebody was keeping score," she said. "Even back then."

"Somebody's always keeping score," said Pip. "That's rather the point of you being here."

chapters.heading: Minute 27: The Word Nobody in England Uses
chapters.text:
The fog cleared into a university courtyard, all gray stone and serious young men in long scarves, arguing.

"They're arguing about football?" Mia asked.

"They're arguing about the *rules* of football," Pip said. "**Cambridge, 1848**. Every school in England played its own version — some let you carry the ball, some didn't, some allowed shin-kicking as a legitimate tactic. These students sat down and wrote out the Cambridge Rules, one of the first tries at getting everyone to play the same game."

A student slammed a paper onto a table. "No hacking," he declared, to groans from half the room.

"They're debating whether you're allowed to kick each other," Mia said, delighted.

"Welcome to rule-making," said Pip. "It is never dignified. Half of sports history is grown men arguing about things a referee's whistle solves in two seconds."

Decades blurred past in a flicker of scribbled notebooks and shouted debates, until Pip stopped the scene at a different school hallway, where a boy was calling across the yard to his friend.

"Oi — fancy a game of *assoc* after class?"

"That's it," Pip said, before Mia could ask. "**1880s England**. 'Association football' was the formal name, so schoolboys shortened it to 'assoc,' then to **'soccer.'** You've been saying a nickname this entire time."

Mia raised an eyebrow. "So 'soccer' is just slang that never grew up."

"Most good words are," said Pip. "I'd watch your tone, by the way. I'm not exactly a formal institution myself."

Mia glanced sideways at the chalk-outline referee currently standing in 1880s England, discussing linguistics with a fifteen-year-old in pajama bottoms, and decided Pip had a point.

chapters.heading: Minute 38: The Rulebook That Stuck
chapters.text:
They landed in a smoky tavern room in London, where a dozen serious men sat around a long table covered in papers.

"This is the big one," Pip said. "**October 26, 1863**. These men are founding **the Football Association** — the FA — and about to decide something that will outlast every single one of them."

One man stood, holding a sheaf of paper like it was a verdict. "No carrying the ball," he announced. "If your hands touch it, play stops."

"**Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Pip said quietly. "He wrote the first official Laws of the Game himself, right down to the size of the pitch. The rulebook soccer still uses, in its bones, today."

Mia studied the room. Something in the stack of papers caught her eye — a column of scrawled scores from scrimmage matches the men had clearly used to test the rules before locking them in.

"They play-tested it," she said. "Like, actually ran the numbers first."

"Every good rule gets tested," Pip said. "Even the offside law gave people headaches for a century afterward."

Pip flicked forward through the years like turning pages, pausing on a muddy field crowded with spectators in bowler hats, watching a plain silver cup get held up.

"The **FA Cup**," Pip said. "First played in **1871 and 1872**. It's the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world. Clubs have been fighting over it for more than a hundred and fifty years."

Mia watched the trophy get lifted to a roar of cheering. "A hundred fifty years of the same tournament," she murmured. "That's basically the oldest dataset in sports."

"Careful," said Pip. "Keep talking like that and I'll put you on the rules committee."

chapters.heading: Minute 50: The First International, and the League That Followed
chapters.text:
The tavern dissolved into open gray sky and a roaring crowd packed along a Scottish field.

"**Glasgow, 1872**," Pip said. "The first official international match ever played. Scotland against England."

Mia watched the game unfold — tense, tight, both sides defending like their lives depended on it. When the final whistle blew, nobody had scored.

"Wait, that's it?" Mia said. "Nil-nil?"

"**Nil-nil**," Pip confirmed. "The very first international soccer match in history, and it ended in a scoreless draw. Somewhere, a stats student is nodding right now."

"I would never be that smug," Mia said, visibly being that smug.

Pip moved them on, through sixteen years in a blink, to a smoky meeting hall where a stocky man with a notebook was arguing passionately with a room of club officials.

"**William McGregor, 1888**," Pip said. "He got twelve clubs to agree to play each other on a fixed schedule, every team, home and away, with a running table to track it all. The world's first football league."

Mia's eyes lit up at the word "table." "So he basically invented the standings page."

"More or less," said Pip. "People have been refreshing it obsessively ever since, you included."

One more jump — Paris this time, a small office, seven men signing a document around a single candle.

"**1904**," said Pip. "Seven countries founding **FIFA**, football's world governing body. The organization that will eventually run the tournament you've definitely stayed up far too late watching."

Mia smiled. "Guilty."

"Four years from here, it's this meeting's job to invent a World Cup," Pip said. "But first — I want to show you something this sport nearly lost entirely."

chapters.heading: Minute 63: The Ban, and the Comeback
chapters.text:
The light shifted to a packed stadium in the north of England, bigger than Mia expected, full of roaring fans.

"This can't be men's football," Mia said, studying the kits.

"It isn't," said Pip. "This is the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, one of the most popular teams in England during the First World War, when the men's leagues had paused. Fifty thousand people came to watch them play on Boxing Day, **1920**."

On the field, a player cut past two defenders with a touch so clean Mia actually gasped.

"**Lily Parr**," Pip said. "Their biggest star. Helped make this team impossible to ignore."

Mia leaned forward, grinning — and then the scene darkened, the stands emptying, a notice nailed to a gate reading simply: WOMEN NOT PERMITTED.

"In **1921**, the FA banned women's football from its grounds," Pip said, voice flat. "No real reason that held up. They just decided the game wasn't 'suitable.' It lasted **fifty years**."

Mia's jaw tightened. "That's not a rule. That's just taking the ball away because you don't like who's winning."

"It was unfair," Pip agreed simply. "Nobody involved pretends otherwise."

But Pip kept moving, and the gate dissolved into a bright modern stadium, bunting flying, a scoreboard reading **1971**.

"The ban was finally lifted," Pip said. And twenty years after that, the scene shifted again — floodlights, a packed arena in China, a roaring crowd.

"The first official **Women's World Cup** was held in **1991**," Pip said. "The United States won it."

Mia watched the American players lift the trophy, chills running down her arms despite the warmth of the lights.

"Fifty years is a long time to wait for a kickoff," she said quietly.

"It is," said Pip. "Which is exactly why the people who kept showing up anyway matter so much."

chapters.heading: Minute 75: A Trophy, a Theft, and a Very Good Dog
chapters.text:
Pip set them down on a sun-baked dock in South America, crowds cheering as a ship unloaded crates.

"**Uruguay, 1930**," Pip said. "The first ever **FIFA World Cup**. Host nation against the world."

Mia watched the final whistle blow on a packed stadium, the home crowd erupting. "Uruguay beat Argentina," Pip confirmed, "in the final, in front of their own fans."

Pip held up a small golden statue, a woman holding an eight-sided bowl above her head.

"This is what they played for," Pip said. "FIFA president **Jules Rimet** pushed the whole tournament into existence, and this first trophy carried his name."

Mia turned the little statue over in her hands — then it vanished, and they were standing on a London street in **1966**, outside an exhibition hall.

"Something's wrong," Mia said, reading a dropped newspaper: TROPHY STOLEN.

"Someone walked off with the World Cup itself," Pip confirmed, "right here in London, a week before the tournament kicked off."

"Did they catch him?"

"Didn't need to," Pip said, smiling. "A week later, a dog out on a walk found the trophy wrapped in newspaper under a hedge. His name was **Pickles**."

Mia laughed so hard she nearly sat down in the street. "The actual World Cup was found by a dog named Pickles?"

"PICKLES FOUND IT," Pip announced, with the enormous satisfaction of a referee who has waited years to say that sentence out loud. "**England went on to host and win that 1966 tournament** — their only title to this day. Some say Pickles deserved a medal more than the defenders."

Mia grinned at the thought of a dog on a podium. "I'd have flagged that as a major outlier in my model."

"Most good stories are," said Pip.

chapters.heading: Minute 88: Three Stars and a Yellow Card
chapters.text:
They landed in Mexico, **1970**, heat shimmering off a packed stadium, a player in bright yellow gliding past defenders like they weren't there.

"**Pele**," Pip said. "Brazilian forward. Watch."

Mia watched him drag the ball one way, send two defenders the wrong direction, and finish calmly into the corner. The crowd didn't just cheer — they seemed to exhale, like they'd been holding their breath.

"That's not fair," Mia said, delighted. "Nobody should be allowed to make it look that easy."

"Brazil has won the World Cup more than anyone — **five times**: **1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, and 2002**," Pip said. "Pele is the only player ever on three of those winning squads — **1958, 1962, and 1970**."

Mia did the mental math instantly. "He won his first one at what, seventeen?"

"Seventeen," Pip confirmed. "Try not to feel behind schedule."

On the sideline, a referee reached into his pocket and held up a small square of bright yellow card — and then, in a different match entirely, flickering past, a red one.

"**Ken Aston**," Pip said. "A referee who got the idea sitting at a traffic light. Red means stop. Yellow means slow down and think about your choices. They debuted right here, at this **1970 World Cup**."

"Every referee in the world owes him a coffee," Mia said.

One last flicker — Brazil's captain lifting the original golden trophy for the third time, and Pip's voice went almost fond.

"Brazil got to keep that first trophy for good, after this third win," Pip said. "**FIFA had to build a brand new one in 1974.**" A pause. "Turns out being too good is its own kind of problem."

Mia looked at the trophy gleaming under the stadium lights, and thought about her spreadsheet waiting back home — every one of these moments eventually reduced to a single line of data that nobody watching live had ever quite believed would happen.

"I don't think I want to put any of this in a spreadsheet," she said.

"Funny," said Pip. "That's usually the exact moment people become historians instead of stat-keepers."

chapters.heading: Full Time
chapters.text:
The stadium noise folded away like a whistle cutting through a crowd, and Mia was back on her bedroom floor, laptop glowing softly, the spreadsheet exactly where she'd left it.

Pip was gone — but the brass whistle on her desk was still faintly warm, and when she picked it up, she found a single word scratched into the metal that hadn't been there before: *ASSOC*.

Mia smiled and checked the clock: 12:14 a.m. It felt like she'd been gone two thousand years, and also no time at all, which was exactly the kind of math her stats teacher would say was impossible and her night would say otherwise.

She opened her spreadsheet back up, but instead of closing it, she added a new tab. She labeled it *Players Who Didn't Get Enough Credit*, and typed one name at the top: **Lily Parr**.

Then, underneath, a second name, because some data points deserve to be remembered even when nobody expects them in the dataset: **Pickles the dog**.

She sat there a moment longer, whistle still warm in her palm, thinking about a muddy field in 1314, a scoreless draw in Glasgow, a fifty-year ban that never should have happened, and a seventeen-year-old who had already won a World Cup before most people had picked a college major.

Her own team had two matches left this season. She closed the laptop, finally, and tucked the whistle under her pillow like a lucky charm, half-expecting it to hum again before morning.

Tomorrow, she had a model to finish. But for the first time, she wasn't just counting goals. She was counting who got left out of the story, too — and making sure, this time, they made the final tally.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had a model to finish — and a whole new tab to fill in.

story.title: Theo and the Race to the Moon
story.subtitle: A Roblox Studio glitch turns into the greatest build log in history.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Beep From Nowhere (1957)
chapters.text:
Theo was still awake at midnight, cross-legged on his bedroom carpet, laptop balanced on a pillow. He was building a rocket launchpad for his newest Roblox game, and the countdown animation kept breaking. Every time he hit play, the rocket parts drifted apart like they'd forgotten they were supposed to be a rocket.

This was takeoff attempt number nine. Attempt eight had sent the booster spinning cheerfully into a cloud. Attempt seven had just become modern art.

"Stay together," he muttered, nudging a block back into place.

The screen flickered black, then a sickly green, like his laptop had caught a cold. A chat box popped open where no chat box should be.

RENDERING... RENDERING... HOLD STILL, it said.

A blocky little cube dropped out of the corner of the screen and landed on his desk, humming like a loading bar. It had stubby legs, a crack of a mouth, and a nametag that flickered between PATCH and patch_v2_FINAL_final.

"Your rocket script is wrong," Patch said, in a voice like a dial-up modem clearing its throat. "You're missing the reference build. The original. I can show you."

"Show me what?"

"The first thing humans ever launched that actually stayed up," Patch said. "Before you build it, you should probably see it."

The room folded like a screenshot zooming in, and then Theo was standing — somehow — under a sky full of radio towers, in a year that was definitely not this one.

A small gray ball sat on a workbench nearby, bristling with four thin antennas like a spider that had given up on legs.

"That's it? That's the big launch?"

"That," Patch said, "is Sputnik 1. Launched October 4, 1957, by the Soviet Union. First man-made object to ever circle the Earth."

"It's tiny."

"About 58 centimeters wide," Patch said. "Roughly the size of a beach ball. Didn't need to be big. It just needed to beep."

Right on cue, the ball let out a thin, steady beep... beep... beep, looping every second like a metronome stuck in a good mood.

"People all over the planet picked that up on their own radios," Patch said. "Just an ordinary signal, bouncing down from space for anyone who tuned in."

Theo listened to the loop a few more times, timing it in his head the way he timed respawn sounds in his own games.

"It's a loop," he said slowly. "Like a sound file set to repeat forever."

"Exactly like that," Patch said, actually sounding impressed. "You've basically just reverse-engineered the first satellite."

Theo grinned, already picturing his launchpad script with a beeping loop instead of the glitchy silence it had now. "Can I use this?"

"You're about to see the whole game," Patch said. "This is just Level 1."

The sky rippled, and the little beeping ball shrank into a single bright pixel, pulling Theo forward into the dark.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Dog, the Belt, and the New Team (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
Theo landed somewhere colder, the ground humming under a huge metal gantry. Before he could ask anything, a bark rang out — short, sharp, unmistakably a dog.

"That's... Patch, is there a dog up here?"

"Was," Patch said. "Laika. Launched aboard Sputnik 2 in November 1957. First living creature to ever orbit the Earth."

Theo looked at the little capsule bolted to the rocket's side, smaller than his backpack. "They sent a dog into space before they sent a person?"

"Had to know a living thing could survive the ride first," Patch said. "Laika went first so nobody else had to guess."

Theo didn't say anything for a second. Then he gave the capsule a small, respectful nod, the kind you'd give a teammate who took one for the squad.

The scene rippled forward almost a year, into a room full of men in short-sleeved shirts, staring at chalkboards covered in numbers.

"Sputnik didn't just launch a satellite," Patch said. "It launched a scramble. The U.S. needed its own team, fast."

A banner unrolled across the far wall: a round blue badge with three red bars curling through it.

"NASA," Theo read. "That's the logo from all the rocket documentaries."

"Opened for business October 1, 1958," Patch said. "And less than a year earlier, on January 31, 1958, their very first satellite, Explorer 1, found something nobody expected."

A glowing ring appeared around a cartoon Earth, invisible until Patch highlighted it — a doughnut of fuzzy light circling the planet.

"What is that, a lag glitch?"

"A radiation belt," Patch said. "Invisible bands of tiny charged particles, trapped around the Earth by its own magnetism. Explorer 1 found it completely by accident."

Theo tilted his head, and something clicked for him — the kind of click he got when he finally understood why an invisible wall in his own game kept blocking players from falling off the map.

"It's like a collision box," he said. "You can't see it, but it's still there, still doing something."

"Not a bad way to put it," Patch admitted.

Theo reached toward the glowing ring like he was dragging an invisible brick into place in his own build. "I'm adding one of these. An invisible force field around my planet, so players bounce off instead of floating into nothing."

"Now you're thinking like an engineer," Patch said. "Ready for the next level? This one's got a human in it."

"Finally," Theo said. "Let's go."

chapters.heading: Level 3: 108 Minutes and a Secret Name (1961)
chapters.text:
The next place smelled like metal and nerves. Rows of men hunched over control panels, none of them saying much, all of them watching one clock.

Theo noticed a folded blueprint pinned to the wall, corners curling, signature scribbled in the corner — just two letters, S.K.

"Who's S.K.? Why not just put the whole name?"

"Good catch," Patch said. "That's Sergei Korolev — the chief designer behind almost everything Soviet rockets did. His full name was kept a secret. Most people outside the program didn't even know who he was until after he died, in 1966."

Theo frowned. "They hid the guy who built all this?"

"Space programs had their reasons back then," Patch said. "Point is, some of the smartest people in this story, you never hear their names."

Theo filed that away the way he filed away a good username — the ones that fit better than the real name ever did.

A hatch clanged somewhere above them, and a small spherical capsule shot upward on a column of fire and smoke, loud enough that Theo felt it in his chest.

"April 12, 1961," Patch said, over the roar. "Yuri Gagarin, aboard Vostok 1. First human being to ever leave the planet."

"How long was he up there?"

"One full trip around the Earth," Patch said. "About 108 minutes. Less time than it takes you to finish one of your longer builds."

Theo did the math in his head — 108 minutes was basically one movie, or two recess periods, or exactly the length of time his mom usually gave him before yelling up the stairs about bedtime.

"That's it? He circled the entire planet in less time than a movie?"

"Welcome to orbit," Patch said. "Everything up here moves fast."

The capsule arced overhead, trailing a thin stream of smoke, and somewhere far below a crowd of tiny figures were cheering, waving their arms at the sky.

Theo found himself grinning at a man he'd never meet, in a capsule the size of a trash can, hurtling around a planet at a speed Theo couldn't quite picture.

"Put his initials in your game," Patch said. "Hidden, somewhere nobody would look first. Like Korolev's name. Let somebody find it."

"An easter egg," Theo said slowly. "I can do an easter egg."

"Then you're learning faster than I expected," Patch said, and the sky folded again.

chapters.heading: Level 4: Fifteen Minutes, One Promise (1961)
chapters.text:
A countdown was already running when Theo arrived, red numbers ticking down on a screen the size of a garage door.

"Are we watching another orbit?"

"Not quite," Patch said. "Watch the shape of the flight."

The capsule launched — Theo caught the name stenciled on its side, FREEDOM 7 — and arced up, up, and then, almost immediately, back down, like a kicked ball that never quite cleared the crossbar.

"That's it? It didn't even go around?"

"Alan Shepard, May 5, 1961," Patch said. "First American in space. But you're right. His flight went up and came back down. It never orbited the Earth at all."

"So Gagarin's lap was a whole orbit, and this was just up and down?"

"Exactly the difference," Patch said. "Orbit means you go all the way around, moving fast enough to keep falling past the Earth instead of into it. Shepard's flight was short. Just up, over, and down again."

Theo thought about free kicks, about the difference between a shot that curled all the way into the net and one that sailed over the bar for a throw-in. Same stadium. Very different result.

"Still counts," Theo said. "First American up there has to count for something."

"It counted for plenty," Patch said. "Twenty days later, it counted for this."

The scene shifted to a stage, a man in a dark suit standing at a podium, microphones bristling in front of him like antennas.

"On May 25, 1961," Patch said, "President Kennedy stood up and told the country they were going to land a person on the Moon, and bring him home safe, before the decade was out."

Theo stared at the stage. "That's such a huge promise. What if it hadn't worked?"

"Then a lot of people would've looked very silly," Patch said. "Good thing they didn't stop there."

Theo looked back at Freedom 7, small and sturdy, parked on its launch stand like the very first level of a very long game.

"Two modes," Theo muttered, half to himself. "Quick launch, up and down, short flight. And full orbit, for when you want the real thing."

"Add both," Patch said. "Some players just want the fifteen-minute version."

chapters.heading: Level 5: Forty-Eight Laps (1963)
chapters.text:
The next stop had a number glowing on every wall, counting upward: 1... 2... 3...

"What's counting?"

"Laps," Patch said. "Watch."

A capsule swept past overhead, trailing light, and the number on the wall ticked up again.

"June 16, 1963," Patch said. "Valentina Tereshkova, first woman in space. She used to work in a factory before she trained to fly. That morning, she became the only woman ever to fly a solo space mission."

Theo watched the number climb. 12. 20. 31.

"How high does it go?"

"Keep counting," Patch said.

Theo did, lips moving slightly, the way he counted penalty-kick run-ups before a shot.

"Forty-eight," he said finally, as the number stopped. "She went around Earth forty-eight times?"

"Forty-eight full orbits," Patch said. "More time in space, all at once, than every American astronaut up to that point, combined."

Theo whistled, low. "That's not a quick launch. That's a whole marathon."

"Space doesn't really do halfway," Patch said.

Theo watched the capsule glint past one more time, and an idea nudged at him, the kind that always showed up right before he rebuilt half a level.

"My game needs a lap counter," he said. "Not just 'you reached orbit.' A real score. How many times you go around before you land. People will keep playing just to beat their own number."

"That's called a high score," Patch said. "Pretty sure humans invented those before video games did. Tereshkova just happened to set a very good one."

Theo laughed, and the counter on the wall froze at 48, glowing like something worth remembering.

"Next level's a little more hands-on," Patch said. "Hope you're not scared of heights."

"I build floating platforms for a living," Theo said. "Try me."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Ten Minutes Outside (1965)
chapters.text:
Something drifted past the window before Theo even registered where he was, a long white cord, slack, curling slowly in nothing.

"Is that a leash?"

"Close," Patch said. "A tether. A cord that keeps you attached to your spacecraft, so you don't drift off into nothing."

Beyond the window, a figure in a puffy white suit floated free, utterly alone against a black so complete it looked painted on.

"March 18, 1965," Patch said. "Alexei Leonov, first person to ever leave his spacecraft and float outside it. That's called a spacewalk."

"How long was he out there?"

"About ten minutes," Patch said.

Theo watched the tether stretch taut, then slacken, as the figure drifted and was gently reeled back in like a kite coming home.

"Ten minutes doesn't sound long," Theo said. "But out there, with nothing but a cord?"

"Ten minutes is a very long time," Patch agreed, "when the only thing between you and forever is a rope."

Theo thought about every time he'd built a floating arena in Roblox Studio and forgotten to put a wall around the edge, the number of test players who'd calmly walked straight off into the void because nothing stopped them.

"I need a tether mechanic," Theo said suddenly. "Right now my players can just fall off the edge of my space level and that's it, they're gone. What if instead there's a cord? You can still go explore, but it pulls you back before you really mess up?"

"A built-in save," Patch said. "Not the worst idea you've had tonight."

"I have good ideas all the time," Theo said. "You just keep showing up during the good ones."

"Funny how that works," Patch said, and the tether outside the window snapped taut one more time, reeling the drifting figure safely back through the hatch.

chapters.heading: Level 7: Taller Than Liberty (1968)
chapters.text:
The next level didn't start with a sound. It started with a shadow, a long one, falling across Theo's shoes, like a building had decided to stand directly over him.

He looked up. And up. And up.

"That," Patch said, "is a Saturn V. 363 feet tall. Taller than the Statue of Liberty, base to torch."

"That's not a rocket," Theo said. "That's a skyscraper that caught fire on purpose."

"Designed by a team led by Wernher von Braun," Patch said. "He'd built rockets long before NASA existed, and then spent years helping build this one, the rocket that finally had enough muscle to reach the Moon."

Theo craned his neck, trying to picture the thing lifting off, and mostly failing, the way he failed to picture numbers bigger than his own school's population.

"Where's it going?"

"Watch," Patch said, and the scene swept up, past the rocket, past the clouds, past the blue curve of the Earth itself, until there was nothing below them but a gray, cratered ball.

"December 1968," Patch said. "Apollo 8. First humans ever to orbit the Moon."

A window framed a view Theo had seen a hundred times in photos without ever really seeing it: a half-lit Earth, blue and white and small, rising over the gray edge of the Moon like a sunrise that had gotten its planets mixed up.

"Astronaut William Anders took that picture," Patch said. "They call it Earthrise."

Theo stared at it longer than he meant to. It looked less like a photo and more like something that shouldn't have been possible to take at all, Earth, whole, fitting inside one small frame.

"I want a photo mode," Theo said quietly. "In my game. Something that lets you just stop, and look at the planet, and take a picture of it. Not for points. Just to have it."

"Not every feature needs a leaderboard," Patch said.

"Yeah," Theo said. "Some things you just want to keep."

chapters.heading: Level 8: One Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
The ground here was gray and powdery, and gravity felt wrong, too light, like someone had turned down the setting by accident.

"Where—" Theo started, then noticed the flag, planted stiff in dust that had never once felt wind.

"July 20, 1969," Patch said. "Apollo 11. Go ahead. Look up."

A boot came down slowly, kicking up a small, silent puff of gray dust, and a voice crackled out of nowhere, tinny and calm.

"That's one small step for man," the voice said, "one giant leap for mankind."

"Neil Armstrong," Patch said. "First person to ever walk on the Moon."

Theo watched the boot settle, watched the footprint stay perfectly sharp in dust that had no wind to blur it.

"Is he up here alone?"

"Not quite," Patch said. "Buzz Aldrin joined him down here on the surface. And Michael Collins stayed up in orbit the whole time, alone, flying the command module, Columbia, around and around the Moon, waiting for the other two to finish and come back up."

Theo looked from the two figures bouncing carefully across the gray ground to the empty black sky above them, where somewhere, unseen, a third astronaut circled alone.

"That seems like the hardest job," Theo said. "Everybody remembers the guys who walked. Nobody really talks about the guy flying solo laps the whole time."

"Somebody has to fly the getaway car," Patch said. "Columbia doesn't get there and back without him."

Theo thought about his own games, how every build needed somebody running the server behind the scenes, unseen, while everyone else got the screenshots.

"I'm adding a pilot role," Theo decided. "Multiplayer. One person lands, one person stays in orbit keeping everything running. Both jobs matter. Neither one works without the other."

"Columbia would approve," Patch said.

Armstrong's footprint sat behind them, perfect and undisturbed, as the Moon's gray horizon curved away into black.

chapters.heading: Level 9: The Fix and the Handshake (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
An alarm cut through the quiet before Theo even had time to look around.

"What's wrong?"

"1970," Patch said. "Apollo 13. An oxygen tank blew out on the way to the Moon. Lost power. Lost heat. The crew had to turn back without ever landing."

Theo's stomach dropped. "Did they—"

"They made it home," Patch said quickly, before Theo could finish the thought. "Every single one of them. Engineers on the ground figured out a fix using only the parts the astronauts already had on board, and the crew followed it step by step until they splashed down safe."

Theo let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding. "They fixed it from the ground? With stuff that was already up there?"

"No shop. No spare parts delivery," Patch said. "Just people staying calm and working the problem."

Theo thought about every broken build he'd ever rage-quit on, every script he'd deleted instead of debugged, and felt, for the first time all night, a little bit embarrassed.

"That's basically the best debugging story ever," he admitted.

"Between 1969 and 1972, twelve different astronauts walked on the Moon, across six separate landings," Patch said. "Apollo 13 is the one that didn't make it down, and the one everybody remembers for getting everyone home anyway."

The scene shifted one last time, gentler now, two spacecraft drifting slowly toward each other against the dark, hatches lining up with barely a bump.

"July 17, 1975," Patch said. "American and Soviet spacecraft docked together in orbit, locked nose to nose. The crews opened the hatch between them and shook hands."

Theo watched the two crews float through into each other's spacecraft, grinning, swapping something that looked suspiciously like flags.

"That's it? After all that, racing each other to space, to the Moon, they just shook hands?"

"That's exactly it," Patch said. "Turns out the finish line wasn't really a line at all. Just a handshake, with someone you used to call the competition."

The screen rippled, folding light back into pixels, back into a familiar green glow, and then Theo was sitting on his own bedroom carpet again, laptop warm against his knees.

His rocket script sat right where he'd left it, except now, when he hit play, the parts held together. The countdown ticked. The little beep looped exactly the way Sputnik's had.

Down in the corner of his screen, a small blocky icon blinked once, labeled PATCH, pinned permanently into his toolbar like a tool he hadn't known he needed.

"Same time tomorrow?" Theo whispered to the screen.

The icon blinked, just once, which Theo decided to take as a yes.

He saved the file, finally, and closed the laptop.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a free kick to practice, and a whole Moon landing left to code.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Biggest Ship in Belfast (1909–1911)
chapters.text:
Maya was lying on her bedroom carpet after her bath, hair still damp from swim practice, drawing a boat with her blue crayon.

She drew one funnel. Then two. Then three. Her crayon would not stop. It drew a fourth one all by itself.

The paper rippled, just like water in the bathtub. WHOOOOSH! Maya tumbled right off the page and landed on wooden planks, with hammering banging all around her.

"Watch your step," said a man in a leather apron, catching her elbow. "This is Harland and Wolff, the biggest shipbuilding yard in Belfast, Ireland."

Maya blinked up at a ship so huge she couldn't see the end of it. "Is this... my drawing?"

"This is Titanic," the man said proudly. "Her **keel** — that's the strong backbone underneath a ship — was put down in **1909**. We slid her into the water for the very first time, which we call a **launch**, in **1911**."

Maya counted funnels on the real ship, just like her drawing. One, two, three, four.

"Only three have smoke coming out," the man said, winking. "The fourth is just for looks, to make her seem even grander."

"I drew that one by accident!" Maya laughed.

"Good eye. She's **882 feet** long — the biggest ship anyone has ever built, with two sister ships besides."

Maya traced the ship's long side with her finger, grinning. Her drawing had found something true before she even knew it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Walls That Keep the Water Out
chapters.text:
Inside the ship, pipes clanged and workers called to each other. Maya peeked through a round doorway into the metal belly of the ship.

"What are all these walls for?" she asked, pointing at thick metal dividers chopping the inside into little rooms.

"Those are **watertight compartments**," said the man, patting one. "Sixteen of them. If water ever got in through a hole, these walls would trap it in just one room, so the rest of the ship stays dry."

Maya pressed her palm flat against the cold metal. "So the ship can't sink?"

"People call her nearly unsinkable, because of these walls," he said. "Nearly."

Maya noticed that word — *nearly* — and tucked it away like a secret, to ask about later.

She knocked on one of the walls. CLONK. Solid as a castle.

"Good plan," she said slowly. "But only if the walls go high enough, right?"

The man looked surprised at the clever question, then smiled. "You might be onto something, little artist."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Away from Southampton (10 April 1912)
chapters.text:
The scene shifted, and Maya stood on a crowded dock in England, ribbons and hats everywhere. A deep horn blew. HOOOONK!

"Where are we going?" Maya shouted over the noise.

"New York City!" called a sailor, tying off a thick rope. "We leave Southampton today, **10 April 1912** — her very first trip ever, which sailors call a **maiden voyage**."

Maya spotted families hugging goodbye, kids waving handkerchiefs. She waved too, even though nobody could see her.

A paper ticket blew off a bench and landed at her feet. She turned it over — a drawing of the ship, just like hers.

Maya tucked the ticket into her sketchbook. "I want to see everything," she whispered.

The horn blew once more, and slowly, slowly, the biggest ship in the world pulled away from land.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Captain and the Boats
chapters.text:
Maya found a tall man in a dark blue coat standing calm at the front of the ship, in the room where it was steered.

"That's Captain Edward John Smith," said a sailor nearby. "One of the most experienced captains in the whole company."

Maya counted the small boats hanging from ropes along the deck. She counted on her fingers, then ran out of fingers.

"How many people can those hold?" she asked.

"About **1,178**," the sailor said.

Maya looked at the crowds strolling the deck, laughing and playing cards. "That doesn't seem like enough for everyone on such a big ship."

The sailor's smile faded, just a little. "You're right. It isn't."

Maya frowned, worried — but the sailor patted her shoulder gently. "Nothing to fret over tonight. The sea is calm, and the captain is careful."

Maya nodded, but she drew a tiny lifeboat anyway, with a question mark underneath. Something told her this mattered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Night the Sea Turned Cold (14 April 1912)
chapters.text:
The air turned icy. Maya pulled her sketchbook close like a blanket.

At **about 11:40 at night**, a bell rang out. CLANG CLANG CLANG!

"Iceberg!" someone shouted. The ship turned hard, scraping along a huge chunk of ice hidden mostly underwater.

Maya felt the floor shiver, just a little. Then everything went quiet again.

"Is everyone okay?" she asked a sailor rushing past with a lantern.

"We're sending for help," he said. "Come see."

In a tiny room crammed with wires, two men tapped fast on a machine. CLICK-CLICK-CLICKETY-CLICK.

"That's **wireless**," Maya realized. "Radio messages, with no cords at all!"

"These are Jack Phillips and Harold Bride," the sailor said. "They're sending the old help signal, and the brand new one too — **SOS**."

Maya watched the dots and dashes fly out across the dark water, carrying the message to any ship close enough to hear.

"Will someone hear it?" she asked.

Harold grinned at his headphones. "Someone's already answering."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Help Arrives
chapters.text:
Up on deck, people climbed carefully into the lifeboats, lowered down to the dark water one by one. Maya spotted a woman rowing hard, sleeves rolled up.

"That's Molly Brown," a passenger told her. "She grabbed an oar and helped row the whole way. Folks later called her the unsinkable Molly Brown."

Maya noticed something fluffy poking out of a shawl nearby. "Is that a dog?"

"Two little Pomeranian dogs made it into the boats," the passenger said. "Their owners just couldn't leave them behind."

Far off, music drifted across the water, soft and steady. "The band's still playing," someone whispered, "led by Wallace Hartley." That might be a bit of a stretched tale, since nobody is quite sure which songs — but it tells you how brave the players were.

Maya hummed along, even though she didn't know the tune.

Hours passed, cold and quiet, until a light appeared on the horizon.

"CARPATHIA!" a sailor yelled, pointing.

The steamship Carpathia had raced through the night and found the lifeboats floating safely. One by one, everyone climbed up to warm blankets and hot cocoa.

Maya cheered from her own small paper boat. "They made it!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Lost and Found (1985)
chapters.text:
The scene shifted again, and Maya floated above dark blue water that stretched on forever.

"Where's the ship now?" she asked.

A screen on a research ship flickered green, like fuzzy static. A man with kind eyes watched it closely.

"That's Robert Ballard," said a voice behind her. "An explorer who spent years searching the bottom of the sea."

On **1 September 1985**, his team's cameras finally spotted something huge and rusty, sitting **12,500 feet** down — so deep that sunlight never reaches it.

Maya peered at the picture: a giant shape, broken into two big pieces, resting **370 miles** off the coast of Newfoundland, Canada.

"It's like finding something nobody could reach for years and years," Maya whispered.

"Just as exciting to find, too," Ballard said, smiling.

Maya reached toward the glowing picture, and it rippled, just like her sketchbook always did.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The water-light faded, and Maya landed back on her bedroom carpet with a soft FLUMP.

Her sketchbook lay open in her lap, pages warm, as if they had just been swimming.

"What happened after?" she whispered to the last glowing line of ink.

Words formed gently across the page: after that night, people made a new rule — every ship had to carry enough lifeboats for every single person on board, always. Lookouts began watching extra carefully for ice, too.

Maya smiled, tracing the words with her finger. "So the next ships got to keep everyone safe."

On her desk sat a drawing she didn't remember finishing: a lifeboat, full to the brim, rowing safely toward a bright little steamship.

Maya pulled her blanket up to her chin, boat dreams and swim-practice dreams mixing together.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Sleep tight, little sailor.

story.title: Zara and the Ember Geode
story.subtitle: A rockhound's tour through Earth's fieriest mountains

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rock That Breathed Fire
chapters.text:
Zara lined up her rocks on the carpet, biggest to smallest, the way she did every single night before bed. Her newest one sat at the very end — a lumpy gray rock she'd found by the back fence, still gritty with yard dirt.

Tonight, it was warm. Not a little warm. It glowed, faint and orange, pulsing slow like a tiny heartbeat trapped inside the stone.

"Rocks don't do that," Zara whispered, scooting closer on her knees.

"This one does," said a small, crackly voice. A seam split open along the rock's side like a sleepy eye blinking awake. Out climbed a tiny creature made of shiny black stone, with soft orange light flickering under its skin like a nightlight that never quite switched off.

"I'm Cinder," it said, dusting grit off its shoulders. "This is the Ember Geode. Want to see where I'm from?"

Before Zara could answer, the rock cracked wide, pouring warm orange light across her bedroom floor. The carpet melted away. In its place rose a mountain, smoking gently at its top, under a sky that didn't look like her sky at all.

"That," said Cinder, pointing up, "is a **volcano** — an opening in Earth's hard outside shell, called the **crust**, where hot melted rock, smoke, and gas can escape."

"Melted rock? Like melted crayons left on the radiator?"

"Kind of like that," said Cinder, grinning. "Underground, we call that melted rock **magma**. The second it spills out on top, where the sky can see it, we call it **lava**. Same stuff. New name, once it arrives somewhere people can watch."

Zara reached toward the glow, and Cinder gently caught her hand before she got too close.

"Watch first," he said. "Touch never."

Zara nodded and grabbed Cinder's warm little hand instead. "Show me everything," she said.

"Everything" was a very big order. Cinder's glow brightened, like he'd been waiting years for someone to ask exactly that.

"Hold on tight, rock star," he said. "We're headed for the ring."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ring That Isn't Round
chapters.text:
They landed on a cloud of warm mist, floating above a map made of glowing lines. Zara gasped. The lines curved into a giant horseshoe shape, wrapped most of the way around a wide blue ocean.

"That's the **Ring of Fire**," said Cinder. "Horseshoe-shaped, even though its name says 'ring.' It runs almost all the way around the **Pacific Ocean**."

Zara traced the curve with her finger. Everywhere she touched, a tiny volcano blinked on, like a firefly waking up. One, two, three — she lost count somewhere past twenty.

"That one line holds about **three out of every four** volcanoes on the whole planet," said Cinder. "One country along it, called **Indonesia**, has more active volcanoes than anywhere else on Earth."

"Why here?" Zara asked. "Why not everywhere?"

"Earth's crust isn't one solid piece," Cinder explained. "It's cracked into giant puzzle pieces called **plates**, and they're always moving — slow as a snail, but never stopping. Where they bump together, pull apart, or slide past each other, volcanoes like to pop up."

Zara pressed two rocks together in her palm, the way she imagined the plates might squeeze. One corner lifted with a tiny scrape.

"That's it exactly," said Cinder. "Nicely squeezed, rock star."

Zara studied the glittering horseshoe of lights floating above her, and felt a little thrill, the kind she got right before opening a geode. "Which one do we visit first?"

She scanned the whole map, past the busy, crowded edges, and pointed instead at a small cluster of lights sitting right in the blank blue middle, nowhere near a single crack.

Cinder tilted his head, surprised. "Curious choice. Good eye, actually — that's a strange one. Let's go find out why."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Gentle Giant of Hawaii
chapters.text:
The mist cleared into bright blue sky, and the smell of warm rock drifted past. Below them, rivers of orange lava oozed slowly down a wide, gently sloped mountain, like syrup down a short stack of pancakes.

"This is **Kilauea**," said Cinder, "in Hawaii. It's been letting out lava almost nonstop for decades — one of the busiest volcanoes anywhere on Earth."

Zara tilted her head. "But you said volcanoes live at the edges of those puzzle pieces. This isn't an edge."

"Sharp memory," said Cinder. "Most volcanoes don't. This one's special. Deep under Hawaii sits a **hotspot** — a patch of extra-hot rock rising up through the middle of a plate, instead of its edge. No cracking needed at all."

Zara studied the mountain's shape: wide, and low, nothing like the pointy triangle volcanoes in her coloring books.

"It's not pointy," she said. "It's more like a shield. Like the one on my knight costume."

"Exactly right," said Cinder, grinning so hard his glow flickered. "We call that shape a **shield volcano** — wide, with gentle slopes, because its lava is thin and runny, and spreads out flat instead of piling up steep."

Zara felt a puff of warm air drift up from the mountain, from a safe distance Cinder insisted on, and it ruffled her hair like a hairdryer.

"It tickles," she giggled.

"Wait until you see its neighbor," said Cinder. "Want to guess how big?"

Zara's eyes lit up instantly. Guessing was her favorite game in the whole world, better even than hide and seek.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Stacking a Mountain
chapters.text:
"Guess first," said Cinder, "using your rocks."

Zara pulled a handful of extra rocks from her pockets — she always kept spares, just in case — and stacked them into a wobbly tower on a flat stone.

"This is my tallest mountain ever," she announced, as the tower reached past her knee before toppling sideways with a clatter.

Cinder laughed, a sound like pebbles shaking in a tin can. "Good try. Now imagine that tower, but **over four thousand meters** tall. That's taller than four thousand of your bedrooms, stacked straight up to the sky."

Zara's mouth fell open. "That's not a mountain. That's a sky-scraper made entirely of rock."

"Meet **Mauna Loa**," said Cinder, as the mist parted to show the biggest mountain Zara had ever seen, its peak lost somewhere in the clouds. "It's the largest active volcano on the whole planet, just by how much mountain there is to it."

"Is it a shield too?" Zara asked, remembering Kilauea's gentle slope.

"Good memory," said Cinder. "Same wide, gentle shape. Just a lot more of it, piled up over a very long time."

Zara pressed her palm flat against the warm ground at its base and imagined it going up and up, past the clouds, further than her tower had ever dreamed of going.

"I want to build one like this with blocks when I get home," she said.

"You'll need a very big floor," said Cinder. "And a very patient grown-up."

Zara giggled, scooped her fallen rocks back into her pocket, and let Cinder tug her sleeve toward the next stop — somewhere much, much older than this one.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Letter Across the Bay
chapters.text:
The sky had gone strange and dim here, even though Cinder promised it was still daytime. A tall, pointy mountain smoked quietly in the distance, over a sparkling blue bay.

"This is **Vesuvius**, in Italy," said Cinder, his voice softer than before. "A very long time ago, in the year **79**, long before your great-great-great-grandparents were even born, it erupted hard and buried two whole towns — **Pompeii** and **Herculaneum** — under thick, heavy ash."

Zara's eyes went wide, but Cinder gave her hand a gentle squeeze.

"The story people remember best from that day," he went on, "is about someone who watched safely, from across the water, far from any danger."

"Who?"

"A Roman writer named **Pliny the Younger**," said Cinder. "He watched from a safe distance and wrote letters describing exactly what he saw — a huge cloud shaped like an umbrella pine tree, shooting way up into the sky."

"He wrote it down instead of running?" Zara said.

"He was already safe, so he watched, and he wrote," said Cinder. "Scientists still read his letters today. They even named this kind of big, explosive eruption after him — a **Plinian eruption**, right there in the science books."

Zara thought for a moment, then pulled a crumpled paper and a crayon stub from her pocket — she kept those too, just in case — and scribbled a wobbly mountain with a puffy cloud on top.

"I'm writing my letter too," she announced proudly. "Dear Nobody. I saw a volcano today. It was enormous, and also a little bit scary, but I was far away and totally fine."

Cinder read over her shoulder, his glow warm with something like pride.

"Pliny would absolutely approve," he said. "Let's go find you something loud to write about next."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Loudest BANG
chapters.text:
They landed on a quiet beach, which seemed like an odd place for the loudest chapter yet.

"In **1883**," said Cinder, "an island volcano called **Krakatoa** exploded so loudly that people heard the BANG almost **three thousand miles away**, on another island clear across the ocean."

Zara tried to picture that. "That's like if I shouted in my backyard, and Grandma heard me in a different country."

"That's exactly like that," said Cinder.

Zara cupped both hands around her mouth. "CAN YOU HEAR ME?" she bellowed, as loud as her lungs would allow.

A flock of seabirds scattered off the rocks nearby. Cinder's glow wobbled with laughter.

"Not quite three thousand miles," he said, "but a very respectable effort for a Tuesday."

"How do people even know it was THAT loud?" Zara asked.

"People wrote it down, all over the world, the very same day," said Cinder. "Ships' logs, newspapers, letters, all describing a strange boom they couldn't explain, thousands of miles from Krakatoa. Scientists pieced the puzzle together afterward."

Zara looked out at the calm, ordinary-looking water. "It doesn't look like anything happened here at all."

"Lots of time has passed," said Cinder gently. "The ocean tidies up. But the sound still traveled farther than any sound ever recorded before or since, right across this very water."

Zara picked up a smooth black pebble from the sand and turned it over in her fingers before tucking it carefully into her pocket, right next to her letter to Nobody.

"Souvenir," she explained, when Cinder raised an eyebrow. "Every good trip needs one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain That Lost Its Top
chapters.text:
The ground gave a tiny shiver under Zara's sneakers, so small she almost missed it.

"Did you feel that?" she asked.

"Good catch," said Cinder. "Tiny shakes like that are exactly what scientists watch for. They use machines called **seismographs** — boxes that feel even the smallest wobbles in the ground — to notice when a sleepy volcano might be waking up."

Ahead of them stood a mountain with a strange, lopsided top, as if someone had taken a giant bite out of one side.

"This is **Mount St. Helens**, in the United States," said Cinder. "On **May 18, 1980**, the whole side of this mountain slid away in the biggest landslide ever recorded. Moments later, the volcano erupted right behind it, and blew about **thirteen hundred feet** clean off the top."

Zara stared up at the gap where the mountaintop should have been. "That's like somebody knocked the lid clean off."

"A very good way to put it," said Cinder. "Scientists had been watching closely for weeks, because of little shakes just like the one you felt. That careful watching is how so many people got to safety in time."

"Did everyone get away?" Zara asked.

"Most people did, because of all that watching," said Cinder. "One devoted scientist named **David Johnston** was studying the mountain up close, to help keep everyone else safe. We remember him kindly for that."

Zara pressed her palm flat on the ground again, feeling for more tiny shivers, proud to be a lookout too.

"I'm watching," she announced. "Nothing sneaky gets past me."

Cinder smiled, his glow steady and warm. "That's exactly the job," he said. "Rock stars make excellent lookouts."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Island That Grew From the Sea
chapters.text:
Cold, salty wind hit Zara's face, and the water below them bubbled like a giant pot of soup left too long on the stove.

"Welcome to **Iceland**," said Cinder, "home to so many volcanoes, for exactly the reason you showed me back at the ring."

Zara remembered pushing her two rocks together. "You mean pulling apart, not pushing?"

"Smart memory," said Cinder. "Iceland sits right where two giant puzzle pieces are pulling away from each other, slow as ever, leaving room for melted rock to rise up through the gap."

Zara pulled two rocks from her pocket and tugged them apart this time, instead of pushing. A thin gap opened between them.

"Just like that," said Cinder, "except underwater, right here, back in **1963**. The ground kept erupting under the waves for so long that a brand new island pushed itself right up out of the sea."

"A whole island? From nothing at all?" Zara's jaw dropped.

"From lava, cooling and piling up, again and again, patiently, until it finally broke the surface," said Cinder. "They named it **Surtsey**. It's still sitting there today, growing a little plant or two."

Zara looked at the bubbling water and tried to imagine solid ground rising out of it bit by bit, as patient as her own wobbly rock towers.

"I want to watch an island grow," she said.

"That one took years," Cinder admitted, "so you might want a comfier chair, and maybe a blanket."

Zara laughed so hard she nearly dropped her rocks, and Cinder caught every single one neatly, like he'd been practicing that trick for a very long while.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Ash in Her Pocket
chapters.text:
The warm orange light swirled around Zara's feet, and before she could ask for just one more stop, the bubbling sea folded itself away into familiar carpet.

"Two last things," said Cinder, his glow dimming gently, sleepy now too. "First — all that ash volcanoes spit out isn't just messy. It breaks down into **wonderful dirt for growing plants**, so good that farmers often choose to live near volcanoes on purpose, ash and all."

"Even after everything it did?" Zara asked.

"Even after," said Cinder. "Volcanoes build as much as they shake up. New islands, new mountains, new dirt for tomatoes next summer."

"What's the second thing?"

"There's one giant, sleepy volcano under a place called **Yellowstone**, in America," said Cinder. "It had a huge eruption once, hundreds of thousands of years ago. Scientists watch it very closely now, and they see no sign at all that it's getting ready to erupt again soon. It's just resting."

Zara nodded, satisfied, and looked down at her own rock collection, back in its tidy line across the carpet, plus one new smooth black pebble, and one scribbled letter to Nobody.

"Oh — one more-more thing, since you like big," Cinder added, his glow flickering with a last grin. "The biggest volcano anyone's ever found isn't even on Earth. It sits on **Mars**, and it's almost **three times taller** than our very tallest mountain."

Zara gasped. "I'm going there NEXT."

"One sleep at a time, rock star," said Cinder, settling back into the Ember Geode. Its glow faded down to something soft and sleepy, more nightlight than furnace.

Zara tucked her new pebble onto the shelf beside her bed, pulled her blanket up to her chin, and gave the little rock a gentle goodnight pat.

"Shine on," she whispered.

From somewhere deep inside it, warm and small, a whisper came back.

"Shine on, rock star."

story.ending_line: Shine on, Zara. Sleep tight, rock star.

facts.text: A volcano is an opening in Earth's crust where hot melted rock, ash, and gases escape from underground.
Molten rock is called magma underground, and lava once it flows out onto the surface.
Most volcanoes form along the edges of Earth's moving plates, where plates push together, pull apart, or slide past each other.
The 'Ring of Fire' is a horseshoe belt around the Pacific Ocean holding about 75% of the world's active volcanoes.
Indonesia has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth.
Hawaii's volcanoes formed over a 'hotspot' of rising hot rock deep inside the Earth, not at the edge of a plate.
Kilauea in Hawaii is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth, erupting almost continuously for decades.
Mauna Loa in Hawaii is Earth's largest active volcano by volume, rising over 4,000 meters above sea level.
Shield volcanoes are wide with gentle slopes, like Hawaii's; stratovolcanoes are tall, steep cones, like Mount Fuji.
Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, burying the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under thick ash.
Roman writer Pliny the Younger watched the Vesuvius eruption and described it in letters, so scientists now call this explosive type a 'Plinian' eruption.
Krakatoa's 1883 eruption made a sound so loud it was heard about 3,000 miles away on Rodrigues Island.
Krakatoa's eruption caused giant tsunami waves that struck nearby coasts, making it one of the deadliest volcanic disasters in history.
In 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia produced history's largest recorded eruption, and its ash helped make 1816 the 'Year Without a Summer' in Europe and America.
On May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens erupted right after the largest landslide ever recorded slid off its side.
The Mount St. Helens eruption blew about 1,300 feet off the mountain's summit while scientists were studying the volcano up close.
Yellowstone sits atop a supervolcano whose last huge eruption happened about 640,000 years ago; scientists see no sign it will erupt soon.
In 1963, a new island named Surtsey rose from the sea near Iceland as an underwater volcano kept erupting.
Iceland has many volcanoes because it sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two of Earth's plates pull apart.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system, about 13.6 miles (22 km) high, nearly three times taller than Mount Everest.
Volcanologists use seismographs to detect tiny earthquakes and satellites to spot ground swelling, both early warning signs of an eruption.
Volcanic ash breaks down into very fertile soil, which is why many farmers live and grow crops near volcanoes despite the risk.
